speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have spent two hours looking through the list and it would seem to be reasonably well in order. However, I should like to take a moment on a point of order. I realize this is not a debatable motion and I do not intend to debate it. I have a very serious suggestion to make to the government House leader and in fact to all hon. members. We have had one parliament in which we have had experience with this method of dealing with the estimates. I have reason to believe we are rapidly approaching the end of another parliament which will be the second experience. There is no doubt in the minds of all hon. members who have participated in committees that we have developed a committee jungle. I am not saying that disparagingly of any party or any hon. member, but it is a fact of life. We have discovered it. Your Honour knows as well as I do the complaints,
Main Estimates, 1973-74
requests, points of order and questions of privilege that have been raised in the House and have made it abundantly plain that this is the case. In addition, an increasingly large number of votes in the estimates are of a legislative nature but are not based on legislation, thereby preventing hon. members from having that opportunity for discussion they would normally have on the second reading, report and third reading stages of a bill.
For these reasons, while we do not intend to oppose this motion-we did toy with the idea-I urge the government House leader to give some consideration to the proposition which has been discussed on a number of occasions that several departments might well be dealt with by the House under conditions that would supply ample safeguards so that there can be a reasonable method of dealing with some of the departments that by their nature need to be discussed in the House as well as in committees.

The supply Standing Orders under which we are working may be a jungle and the committee system may be a jungle, but it was a jungle into which we voluntarily entered as a House of Commons. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on the point of order but my remarks are in a slightly different direction. The point concerns the government House leader and it should also concern the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang). My point of order concerns the requirements of Standing Order 82 (1) having to do with reports and returns which it is mandatory that public officers and private corporations make to the House of Commons. In order to have any intelligent discussion of the estimates, either here or in committee, it seems to me that the law should be complied with and the reports required to be tabled in the House tabled on time.
The Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs tabled its report on January 4 last year for the year ended March 31, 1971. The Department of Energy, Mines and Resources tabled its report on January 30 last year for the year ended March 31, 1971. The Department of External Affairs tabled its report on January 4 of this year for the year ended December 31, 1971. The Department of National Health and Welfare tabled its report on January 4 of this year for the year ended March 31, 1971. The Department of Public Works tabled its report on January 4 of this year for the year ended March 31, 1971. We can see that all of these reports for these departments are at least a year old and should have been tabled a year ago. We cannot have intelligent discussion of estimates under these conditions.
The report on the fitness and amateur sport program was tabled on January 4, 1973, for the year ended March 31, 1971. The report on the Canada Assistance Plan was tabled on January 4 of this year for the year ended March 31, 1971. The report on the Canada Pension Plan was tabled on April 25, 1972 for the year ended March 31, 1971. The report on old age assistance was tabled on June 14, 1972 for the year ended March 31, 1971. The report on the Unemployment Insurance Act was tabled on January 4 of this year for the year ended March 31, 1971.
Here, Sir, my point of order resolves itself into a question of privilege concerning documents which, contrary to the legal requirements, have been tabled late. The Department of Agriculture is to table its report within the first 21 days after a session of parliament commences. It was tabled on February 7, 1973. The Department of Communications is supposed to table its report on or before January 31 following the end of the fiscal year, or within the

first five days of the next session. It was tabled on February 12, 1973. The Department of the Environment did the same, its report being tabled on February 21, 1973. The Department of Regional Economic Expansion also did the same; its report was tabled on February 9, 1973. The Department of the Secretary of State was supposed to table its report within the first ten days of the next session; it was tabled on January 4, 1973, for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1971, and on February 16, 1973, for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1972. This, of course, only treats of departmental reports.
The other day the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) had something to say about his capital budget. According to my reading of the rules, under Standing Order 82(1) the budget of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation should have been tabled at the end of the year, and that has gone by.
We cannot function properly and conduct the business of the House or of the standing committees efficiently unless the government complies with the law and tables these reports as required.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am most grateful to have this opportunity, on behalf of the primary producers in this nation and the processors as well as the allied industries, to speak out at this time on what I believe is one of the gravest injustices perpetrated by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) in his budget when he indiscriminately removed tariffs on foods coming into this country. This was not only a shocking action on his part, but what was equally shocking was the apparent collusion between him and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) on that particular occasion. They seemed to be congratulating each other-as a matter of fact they did shake hands-on a policy concerning the primary producers of this country which will strike at the very heart of many of our farming and processing enterprises in this country which, under the present policies of this government, already operate on a very marginal or non-profit basis.
The agriculture industry is upset to a degree I have never before experienced, not only because of the fact that the tariffs were lowered, but also because as long as two years ago this government approached all the commodity groups in agriculture requesting that they bring forward a careful detailed study on how the tariff problem in respect of GATT might be approached in order that we might grant some concessions that would not injure the industry and gain some concessions in return from the other countries involved. This government which issued this invitation deliberately slapped every commodity group in the face by the action taken on February 19 when it deliberately lowered the tariffs before the results of any of these studies could be made known to the government. Thousands of dollars were wasted, and thousands of hours of study and research were wasted, because of this action on the part of the government. This is the action of a government that derides and criticizes the policy put forward by our party. This is a government which is trying to lay the cause of inflation as well as the high cost of food at the door of the primary producers of agricultural products.
This government is trying to make agriculture the scapegoat for inflation. This is the government which has derived our policy whereby we would seek, in a twopronged attack, to achieve the objective of controlling inflation and prices without putting anybody out of business and without destroying an industry. Our alternative was to lower taxes, provide some incentive for increased 25789-35J

production of food in this country, make it possible for small businesses to survive, give the individual taxpayer more money with which to buy groceries and at the same time introduce some price controls on all items except food. These controls would be imposed for a short period of time in order that we might, in consultation with the provinces, develop guidelines that could provide a reasoned measure of control of inflation about which we are so fearful today. But this government would not even consider such a proposition and pressed the panic button when the latest figures on inflation were brought out. The government indiscriminately lowered the tariff on foods entering this country from offshore. Disruption in the industry and the effect on unemployment will be tremendous.
I do not think the government to this date realizes the trouble it has caused in industry. The minister, in his budget speech, said that he was taking a risk. But, when the government takes a risk, does it have to be a risk that involves the livelihood of farmers and the existence of farms which have been in the same family for three generations? Does it have to be at the risk of small processing companies which have just begun to function on an economic level and which are now having their chances of survival taken away from them? Is this the risk which must be taken? The Minister of Finance said that the Minister of Agriculture would be the watchdog over this program. This minister watched while half the proceeds and profits of the Canadian agriculture industry were swept away in a budget speech. This is the minister who indicated that if this measure should cause any hardship it would be reversed in 24 hours. The occasions on which this government, after having lowered any rate of tariff, ever replaced it have been very few and far between.
The sheep industry of this country, when the tariff was removed on mutton coming into this country from New Zealand and Australia, was assured that if hardship resulted it would be rectified. We do not have any sheep industry in Canada today. It is gone. What does this mean? I am grateful to the hon. member for Peel-Duffer-in-Simcoe (Mr. Madill) for having provided me with this document, and it is from the Peel-Halton Beef Improvement Association. It gives us some indication of what we are up against. The tariff on beef coming into this country was lowered by 1.5 cents a pound. But what does it mean to the primary producer who sells in one year 150 head of cattle, which is not a great number, and there is a great number of producers who sell more? Based on his average return per year, 1.5 cents a pound adds up to the startling sum of $4,800, and that could be the difference between a profit and a loss in the operation of his enterprise.
This government took this action in spite of the fact that the opposite action has been taken by all our trading partners. Do you realize, Mr. Speaker, that the European Economic Community has allocated $3 billion in order to smooth over the bumps experienced by this trading group? Do you realize that of that $3 billion, 86 per cent is directed toward subsidizing agriculture and ensuring that these countries have a viable agriculture industry within the confines of the European Common Market? This is an

February 27, 1973
The Budget-Mr. Danforth
indication of the importance they place on agriculture in those countries. You do not see the Unites States cutting tariffs on food entering that country because, unlike this government, they place a priority on their agriculture. They are not only adopting a policy to protect their agriculture industry now, they are even considering other barriers to stop the inflow of food into their country if there is an indication of damage in the foreseeable future. They are not only dealing with the present, they are dealing with the future, and this is what we need in this country, a long range agricultural policy which we have never had since the government came into office.
The government mentions that this drop in tariffs of 1.5 cents a pound will be passed on to the consumer. This means life or death to the primary producer in many instances, but 1.5 cents a pound, I suggest to you, will never be passed through the whole complicated food chain to the consumer.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Talk about a chaotic policy! I would like to demonstrate what a chaotic policy we have today. We have a government which is making grants for the construction of freezer plants, cold storage, gas storage and common storage. At the very same time they are removing the specific duties, the surcharges, on fruits and vegetables to such a degree that this will shorten the season and make absolutely worthless the economic investment in freezers and in storage in any form. On the one hand, they are telling primary producers to go ahead and buy their policy; on the other hand, they are saying: if you do, we will bankrupt you just that much quicker.
Not only did the government cut these tariffs without consulting anybody in the industry-and I should like to make this point very strongly-but when this policy was adopted, the Minister of Agriculture was not consulted either or else he did not care or understand the ramifications of the drop in the tariffs. I know this Minister of Agriculture. I know his background and I know that this measure was passed without his having been consulted in any way whatsoever. They lowered the tariffs on citrus juices, fruits and vegetables coming into this country at a time when contracts were being negotiated between the processors and the primary producers. I predict that this will have a disastrous effect on these contracts which are being negotiated. The government does not realize what it has done.
I had a phone call from one of the biggest producers of cabbage, a common, everyday staple. He is one of the largest producers of cabbage in my area. As a result of what is considered to be only a slight reduction in tariffs, he decided not to plant one single seed this year because he said that under this program he could not realize a profit. There is a man who is out of business as a result of the policy applied by this government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When the Minister of Finance took this step, it was quite evident to us on this side of the House that he did not understand the tariff structure so far as fruits and vegetables are concerned, a tariff structure which is different from that on other commodities that
are manufactured. When he spoke about specified time periods for the application of a specific duty and then a surcharge, he should remember that these specified time periods were agreed upon by the industry in the 1930's, not in the 1970's. They were agreed upon before research had made it possible for Canadians to extend their production period, both early into the spring and later into the fall, and to develop a greenhouse industry which made it possible for us to produce during the winter months.
Now, what has happened? When the tariff is reduced, what little tariff is left to cover these specified periods results in the cutting off of either the early or the late production. Then, when the surcharges on many of our tender fruits and vegetables were removed, that made it almost impossible for them to be produced at a profit because very often these fruits and vegetables were protected by the surcharge and not by the specific duty. The price structure of the imports was such that the surcharge was much greater than the specific duty. The price of the imported products on an ad valorem basis was much greater, but this was not taken into consideration. What the government has done, when it allowed the inflow by removing the tariff on fresh produce from the United States at a time when we do not have this fresh produce here, has been to run exactly contrary to the interests of our canning industry which processes the produce for which they contracted with the farmers.
This is going to have a serious effect because the processors, to stay in business, will have to make the contracts of payments to Canadian producers low enough to compete with fresh fruits and vegetables coming into the country. This is an almost impossible situation. The tariffs on some of the canned fruits have been lowered to such a degree that the change in tariffs alone, let alone the devaluation of the U.S. dollar, takes every cent of profit out of a case of canned fruit produced in this country. When there is no profit, there is no production.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I regret to interrupt the hon. member, but the time allotted to him has expired.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Eudes Dube (Minister of Public Works):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to be able to take part this afternoon in the debate on the budget.
First of all, I must congratulate my colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) for his excellent budget. It is not only a responsive and responsible budget, but also a generous and a deeply human one.
The area with which I will try to deal in my remarks is the scope, the influence of the budget and of the main programs of the government concerning the economy of the Atlantic provinces, and more particularly of my province of New Brunswick.
In its review of the month of December, the Atlantic Advocate reported a statement of the right hon. Prime Minister which I believe to be quite correct to the effect that "no federal government in the history of Canada has backed up its concern for the welfare of the peoples of the Atlantic provinces with more effort or more dollars than the present government".

February 27, 1973

In human terms, the ideal of equal opportunity for all Canadians is absolutely basic. With that in mind, the equalization payments enable the poorer provinces to provide public services comparable with those of richer provinces.
As we all know, last year the equalization payments amounted to $135 per capita for Nova Scotia, $164 for New Brunswick, $213 for Newfoundland and $215 for Prince Edward Island. Without that generous but fair contribution of the federal government, the Atlantic provinces would simply be unable to give to their citizens a reasonable standard of living for Canadians of our generation.
This is why I was quite pleased to hear the Minister of Finance announce Monday last in the budget that he would increase the equalization payments. The new amount will be paid as new subsidies based on municipal school taxes. And according to that much more generous new formula, the four Atlantic provinces will now receive $194 per capita for Nova Scotia, $218 for New Brunswick, $284 for Newfoundland and $285 for Prince Edward Island. In so far as New Brunswick is concerned, it is an increase of $164 to $214 per capita in one year.
I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that this new federal infusion will contribute largely to the economic development of my province and will enable a greater number of people to remain and prosper in New Brunswick.
In fact, New Brunswick was the only one among the four Atlantic provinces to reverse the periodic exodus of its working people-mostly young-towards other labour markets and to have a net inflow of residents.
As every one knows, Mr. Speaker, the Atlantic provinces have a great deal of natural resources and human wealth. Should the Atlantic wake up, like the Sleeping Beauty, I see no reason why the federal government would not play its role as Prince Charming.
In 1968, we know that the federal government launched a 15-year program of regional economic expansion program to run over a period of 15 years. There are clear signs that the economy is moving along as it has turned a corner and is now going to narrow the economic gap.
Although the unemployment rate is too high in our estimation, its rate for the four provinces is clearly lower than was expected. It has been estimated that, without the massive infusion of federal funds into the region since 1968, the unemployment rate would be 30 per cent above its present figures.
The direct federal grants of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion have generated more than $200 million of investments in new or growing industries, which amounts to about $28 per man, woman and child in the Atlantic region. This will result in 10,000 new jobs.
Another one of the key approach to regional ressources development policy will have been the stimulation and expansion of growth centres capable of accommodating new industries and an expanding population.
Twelve such centres have been identified in the Atlantic provinces, and more than $250 million has already been
The Budget-Mr. Dube
spent by the federal government to enhance the infrastructure.
The benificial federal influence is felt also in the smaller municipalities, small villages, parishes which are not growth centres, through the Local Initiatives Program. And in the framework of the Local Initiatives Program, for the first time in the history of our country, last year our government was directly supporting local projects conceived by people from small communities.
Last winter, and again this winter, you can hear the pound of hammers disturbing the quiet of parish halls, of Canadian Legion premises, of barns and repair shops.
Instead of idling, and being unemployed in all such places people are building, painting, sewing, repairing furniture, helping each other, making positive achievements. In the province of New Brunswick alone, the program has created 24,000 man-months of employment this winter.
Mr. Speaker, during the past five years, the Department of Public Works for one has allocated close to $190 million for various structures in the Atlantic region. I shall mention, for instance, the major tanker terminal at Point Tupper in Nova Scotia and Come-by-Chance, Newfoundland, the ferry-boat wharves at St. John's, New Brunswick and Digby, Nova Scotia.
I should also mention the bridges along the Trans-Canada highway and the international bridges, among them the one between Maine and Saint-Leonard, which is already finished, and the one between Quebec and Flat-lands, New Brunswick, which is under construction.
There is a very impressive list of less spectacular projects that are much appreciated by the local population, such as federal buildings, post-offices, docks and harbours.
Our estimates in the last financial year for maritime building alone amounted to $8,500,000 for the Atlantic area. And as a result of the importance that we attach to small construction to meet the needs of local fishermen, we plan to spend $2 million more on subsidies in the region.
The primary industries in New Brunswick are generally in good shape, Mr. Speaker, as income from agriculture and forestry has held up especially well. On the other hand, it is well known that the pulp and paper industry is still very shaky. In the aim of somewhat lightening the heavy burden under which it labours, the pulp and paper industry is considering installing industrial complexes involving, for example, new sawing techniques, better use of wood residues and the manufacture of products such as plywood. The manufacturing industry will be encouraged to produce equipment for the forest industry, for domestic and for export sale.
In Dalhousie, located in my own Restigouche constituency, paper exports will be facilitated by the construction this year of a new seaport designed to harbour the large modern ships of the Ro-Ro type. On account of the mercury recently discovered in the mud and the waters close to the place that was designated at the very beginning for the construction of the wharf, apparently this wharf will now have to be erected somewhat further up north-east of the first expected location. But we do not

February 27, 1973
The Budget-Mr. Broadbent
anticipate that such a change will delay the construction of the wharf or of the seaport itself.
So, Mr. Speaker, the basic contribution made by the federal government since 1968 has left the Atlantic region poised for dramatic economic achievements in the seventies.
Many changes have vastly improved the climate for economic development. For instance, let us mention the improvement of the highway network all over the Mari-times; I have in mind especially the north of New Brunswick where a generous government grant of $20 million will allow the renovation of Route 11 and its continuation up to Moncton, with much updating. I must also indicate the establishment of the container transportation services at the two main ports in the area, that is St. John, New Brunswick, and Halifax, Nova Scotia. We must also emphasize the development at all levels of the educational and technical services and institutions. We now benefit from a labour force with more education, mobility and flexibility than before thanks due to the programs established to increase workers' mobility and skill, programs that are mainly administered by the federal Department of Manpower and Immigration. Greater resources now provide the industry with the technical and scientific research services heretofore unknown and the assistance provided each provincial government of the Atlantic area permits the planning of community infrastructure, especially in major urban areas.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, the potential for development in the Atlantic area is apparent on account of the tremendous advantage of its geographical situation in relation to the large market on the eastern seaboard of the United States. In the days of super ships in which we live, the deep waters of the Atlantic coast are a more and more valuable asset. Moreover, the environment in our areas is stable and the manpower intelligent and industrious. Congestion does not pose any serious problems and the forms of pollution that exist can be fought and checked at a reasonable cost.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, the government firmly believes in the future of the Atlantic area. The massive federal effort will ultimately bear fruit, there is no doubt about that. Nevertheless, the citizens of that area and all their representatives will have to be more positive and optimistic.
With this in mind, let us recall one of the first visitors to the Maritime provinces, Samuel de Champlain. During the first winter he spent in Nova Scotia, he created l'Or-dre du Bon Temps in order to keep the morale of his officers and soldiers, in the midst of a rigourous winter and depressing circumstances. That Order of Good Time, now known throughout the world, should inspire our deeds and speeches, because positive thinking is father to the powerful results.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, various spokesmen for the New Democratic Party so far in this debate have attempted to indicate, (a) why we are giving general support to the budget and, (b) simultaneously to raise questions about what we would have done

differently had we been in a position not only to influence government but to make the final decisions ourselves. In my few remarks this afternoon, I should like to add some further arguments to this general approach that we have been trying to make as a party.
Before doing so, however, I cannot forgo the pleasure of responding to some of the comments made by the party on my right, the official opposition.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The only opposition.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: At various times they have suggested that the New Democratic Party, because it has decided under the present proposals of the budget to give support, has somehow been lacking in principle.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are right.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They suggest that we are abandoning the objectives that historically our party has fought for in this country. I find that argument rather curious, coming from that motley crew on my right, a party which, if we are to accept the word of the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) as the spokesman for the Conservative party, has at least progressed from the 18th century and Adam Smith as represented historically right up to last week in the speeches of the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert). I ask all members of this House, Mr. Speaker, who is the real voice of the Conservative party? Who speaks for that party today? Is it the hon. member for Don Valley, on the one hand,-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In his position he does.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-who is arguing that what we need is greater deficits, and who is now arguing for the Conservative party something that the New Democratic Party has been advocating for years that we should use our reserves of U.S. dollars to buy back control of certain sectors of the Canadian economy which are currently foreign owned. Up to last week such an argument was heresy in the Conservative party of Canada, yet the hon. member for Don Valley is now coming forward with these suggestions.
The hon. member for Edmonton West conventionally argues for control of inflation and that we must have a balanced budget at all costs. Last year when the foreign takeover bill was before this House he opposed any movement by the government, and therefore the people of Canada, into the foreign-owned sector to gain control of our economy for the people of this country. When the foreign takeover bill is reintroduced I will be interested to see who is the Conservative spokesman; will it be the hon. member for Don Valley or the hon. member for Edmonton West? We could see another historical shift in that party at that time.
The point I am making, Mr. Speaker, is that in this debate the New Democratic Party has not in any way abandoned its principal concern with the redistribution of income and wealth, the redistribution of power in Canada. All its spokesmen have argued consistently in support of this budget.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
To save your necks.
February 27, 1973

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-not because it implements our program but because it at least moves in our direction. There has been no suggestion at all from the Conservative party of a coherent move, whether in our direction or any other. For them to suggest that somehow it is we who have abandoned a principle in our current situation is, to understate it by about 1,000 per cent, a little curious.
What specifically are we supporting, Mr. Speaker, and how would we perhaps have improved, even in those areas had we had the real power as opposed to merely the influence to do it?
First of all, we like that universal minimum $100 tax cut. That is the kind of idea for which we have been arguing for some time. We proposed in an amendment to the budget last year in debate that we have a minimum of $100-in fact, an inclusive $100 tax reduction for everyone. We regard that as a progressive type of proposal as opposed to cuts of a certain percentage right up the scale. With the $500 ceiling proposed in this budget, at least we do not have the across the board percentage reduction all the way up the scale that we had in last year's budget, so that certain taxpayers could save thousands of dollars and those at the bottom of the scale a mere pittance.
How would we have changed it had we had the real power to do so? The kind of thing we would have done would have been to give an across the board $200 tax cut to every taxpayer. We would not have given more than $200 in tax cuts to any one taxpayer in Canada. That seems fundamental to us on grounds of equity or justice. It would have involved a fair redistribution of income and net disposable income available to average and poor Canadians would have risen. We would have removed that $500 limit that is part of the Liberal government's proposal and would have said that nobody will be allowed more than $200, but all will get that $200. So, on grounds of equity and fairness that measure would have been good. Also, it would have stimulated the economy by putting more money into circulation, increasing demand and therefore creating more jobs. According to our research, that measure would have put the same number of disposal dollars into the economy and would have stimulated jobs to the same degree as the present proposal. Furthermore, it would have put money into the hands of those who need it most. We would not have needed to go up to the $500 ceiling in tax cuts which benefits only the upper top 10 per cent of taxpayers in this country. They will really reap the gain of that $500 limit. From our point of view that is unjustified.
Another point I wish to mention has to do with the pension increase. Increasing the basic pension to $100 a month is good. The increase is $14. We support that. However, may I draw something to Your Honour's attention? If you take the level of pensions prevailing in 1952 and consider how much the cost of living has increased since then, how much inflation we have suffered from, how much the dollar has decreased in value, and how much the gross national product has increased since 1952, I submit that the pensioner in Canada today, if he is to maintain his position in the community as it was in 1952, should be entitled to a basic pension of $110. With those considerations in mind, my party would have increased
The Budget-Mr. Broadbent
the pension ceiling and gone well beyond the $100 that the government has adopted. Nevertheless, we welcome the $100. With this increase, we are getting more from the Liberal government than we would have received from a Conservative government, according to what was said in the last election.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are getting exactly the same thing.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) would read the literature his own party put out in the last election.
Next, I shall touch on consumer spending. There has been an average reduction of 5 per cent in tariffs, which is good as far as it goes if it is passed on. This tariff reduction will help the average consumer in an equitable way, and therefore we support that. I think the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) and other government spokesmen have exaggerated rather grotesquely the benefits of this measure. I, for one, see that tariff concession as being aimed at trade negotiations with the United States. I think that is what is really involved. The government took unilateral action of this kind hoping, somehow, to mitigate the hostile feelings of the United States at this time. That country is suffering difficulties in connection with its balance of payments in international trade. The government sought to mitigate hard feelings; that was the real object of that measure even though, as I say, the Canadian consumer is to be given some benefit.
Another item that we support in the budget is the reduction of the 12 per cent sales tax on children's clothing. This is important, particularly for low income families in Canada. This reduction goes towards an important aspect of daily living, in that our people must clothe their children in an adequate way. We support that initiative. Sales taxes are regressive taxes. The same tax in dollars is paid by upper income, middle income and poor families; therefore, this is a regressive form of taxation and, as far as we are concerned, the sooner we get rid of all sales taxes in Canada the better. However, as the government in Ottawa is moving in the direction of eliminating that tax, it is good that it has begun with taking it off children's clothing. I was pleased to see that Eaton's and Simpson's in Toronto, two large merchandisers, have indicated that they will pass the tax savings on to consumers immediately. I hope the taxpayers benefit from similar action by other merchants, and I hope particularly that the Minister of Finance sets up some monitoring body within his department to make sure that these benefits are passed on to consumers.
Another item we support is the increase by nearly 20 per cent in war veterans' allowances. Again, that is overdue. Again, my party unreservedly supports the government on this, as it is something for which we have been arguing enthusiastically for some time.
Next, may I mention a budget item that will go a long way towards improving the tax position of ordinary people in what are regarded as "have-not" provinces of Canada. I am speaking of the change in the equalization payment formula proposed by the federal government. This will take into account the spending at the provincial level on education. May I point out that education funds are largely derived from taxation of property owners, in

February 27, 1973
The Budget-Mr. Rynard
other words, average people, who in most provinces have had to pay a disproportionate part of the education cost through property taxes. By taking this factor into account in the equalization payment formula, the property tax, for example, of the average person in Saskatchewan will be reduced substantially. Speaking as one who comes from a province that, compared with others, is well off and fortunate, I am pleased to see that we are to redistribute income in this way. Therefore, the government deserves credit for the steps it is taking in this direction.
I have indicated my support for the kinds of measures that my party historically has argued for in Ottawa and in the provinces. I have suggested that we would have made definite changes and improvements if we had formed the government. Nevertheless, we are pleased to support steps that the government has taken in that direction. The single most important deficiency in this budget relates to the deficit. We think that the treasury department finally has won, as the government's approach to spending in terms of gross amount has not changed basically since the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was elected in 1968. If we had formed the government, instead of being able to influence in some marginal way those who now make the decisions, we would have doubled that forecast deficit, not only for the next year but for the next five or ten years, so that we could move effectively to cure unemployment. We would not wish to create miracles overnight, and for the short run bring unemployment down to 4 per cent-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member, but his time has expired.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a critical budget. What will it do? Will it do what the government hopes? Last fall, during the election campaign, there were three principal items with which people were dissatisfied, namely, unemployment, inflation and taxes. The public had already seen the inane actions of a government in increasing taxes and limiting credit to stop people buying. That, in the long run, created unemployment, because industry was not able to sell its products. The government's purpose was, of course, that of halting inflation, Mr. Speaker. Instead, we wound up with both unemployment and inflation. This is all a matter of record, regrettably. The people were annoyed. Can you blame them? Tax measures were taking more and more money from pay envelopes, from industry and from business. Mr. Benson's taxation reforms had upset the business world. Business people could not interpret the new laws, and neither could Members of Parliament. Closure choked off debate on this tax legislation after 75 clauses had been passed, and with less than one quarter of the 735 pages of the bill discussed. Hon. members will recall it required 135 amendments to deal with those clauses which were reviewed. What a bureaucratic jungle he wished on the people.
When pressed for tax cuts last May, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) came through with a 3 per cent rebate on income, but only effective until January 1,1973. There will be a pay day here. He reduced corporation taxes, but this was overdue. Corporate taxes could be
PMt. BroacHaent.]
lowered more. In fact, they are down to 35 per cent in Japan. They are also lower in other countries. Profits were running between 5 per cent and 6 per cent and we were asking the Canadian people to invest in Canadian companies. They were running twice as high 20 years ago; in 1964, 20.5 per cent; 1965, 19.4 per cent; 1966, 17.6 per cent; 1967, 14 per cent; 1968, 14.3 per cent and 1971, 12.4 per cent. Our exports were falling relatively and our imports were increasing relatively. The minister knew that 25 cents out of every dollar came from our exports.
The minister also knew that if people were to be induced to invest in Canadian industry, they had to see prospects for returns. In spite of the leader of the New Democratic Party and his corporate rip-offs, people were not rushing to take advantage of this so-called bonanza. If Canadians do not invest, then outside interests will come in. With over 600,000 people unemployed, we need them badly.
How wrong and inept this government has proven itself to be. It was out millions of dollars when predicting its revenues and $1 billion more or less in its calculation of the unemployment insurance fund. If this were a private business, that fellow would get bounced awfully quick for doing such accounting work. The Minister of Finance has been collecting millions of dollars from taxpayers across the country, money to which he had no right. It took an election to show the minister how wrong he had been. According to his own statement, he has now entered the villa of political bankruptcy by lowering taxes. This is something that could have been done months ago when it was proposed by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield).
What did the budget do? Let us take a look at it. It raised the old age security pension to $100 per month. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, this in no way makes up for the increase in the cost of food and shelter since 1963 when the basic pension of $75 was fixed. The country is still cheating these people. Nothing was done about including drugs in the medicare plan, yet this was part and parcel of the Hall Commission Report on National Medicare which a Liberal government introduced. People over the age of 65 require a good deal more prescription medicines than those under that age.
According to the Economic Council of Canada, one in four people today are below the poverty line. The government consistently refuses to help the most needy, the sick and the ailing. The budget did not provide anything for chronic nursing care or anything to prevent the necessity for active hospital care, yet governments scream about the cost of health care and rising hospital costs. They blame the doctors, everyone but the governments who do not provide chronic nursing care for the sick so that patients can be discharged from hospitals. What a mess governments make when they take over administration.
Health care costs will increase 14 per cent this year. The government and the minister say they do not want anyone asking for a raise. We must all show responsibility. The day after the minister said this when presenting the budget the government brought in its own spending estimates, which showed an increase of 17 per cent. This was one day after the minister pleaded with the people of Canada not to ask for a raise. The budget will help with
February 27, 1973

the financing of children's clothing, candy and soft drinks, jewellery and cosmetics, but I wonder what manner of reasoning was used in arriving at this decision when a young couple who want to build a home for those same children find themselves faced with a 12 per cent sales tax on the building materials for that home. Surely, the cost of shelter should not have been overlooked. This sales tax accounts for thousands of dollars in the cost of the house and its financing.
What kind of a deal is this exemption to the farmer and his son when the family farm passes on from generation to generation? If anybody is going to win, it will have to pass on from generation to generation from here to eternity. Very few farms continue to be held by the same family beyond a couple of generations. Let us take an example. A farmer buys a farm for $25,000. On valuation day, it is worth $50,000. The son gets the farm after 20 years, but 10 years after that he has to sell because of urban sprawl, ill health or a dozen other reasons and the price is $100,000. Does the son pay capital gains on $75,000 or $50,000? The government is always the silent benefactor while over the years the farmer was the worker, the caretaker and the one who make the investment. The government can even change the rules before the farm is disposed of finally. If anyone does not believe that, just go back to 1936. The Liberal government of the day pleaded with people to invest in Canada. The government sold what were known as 1936 perpetual bonds which cost 98 cents on the dollar. What can you get for them today? If any member opposite wants to bid 40 cents on the dollar he can have them.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Have you got some, Doc?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, I do not have any. However, I have received many letters from widows and old people who are wondering what in the world to do with them. They thought these would provide a good living for them in their old age. They thought the government would be honest and fair with them, and they would be able to cash them when the coupons ran out. That is what governments do.
Although we welcome the income tax reduction, just what does it amount to? The minister was to increase taxes by 3 per cent on January 1 of this year, so in effect I suggest the 5 per cent reduction is really only 2 per cent. The minister also said that he was going to take three-quarters of a million people off the tax roll, and I am sure some hon. members of the House remember what a former minister, Edgar Benson said. He said that he was going to take three-quarters of a million people off the tax rolls and he did, but within a year they were nearly all back on the roll again paying taxes. The Minister of Finance has now done a flip and is putting three-quarters of a million people off the roll who will all be back again within a year or so.
Has the minister lowered taxes sufficiently that the people can spend more, and more jobs will be created? That is the burning question. If he has, then are controls necessary to hold the line? The public is losing faith in the ability of governments, governments that blunder. The budget is complicated. Its end results are not certain and
The Budget-Mr. R. Caouette
the new tax forms are so complicated that the public just does not understand them. The public is in rebellion. People want a better accounting system, a simple system so that they will understand what goes on and may judge whether or not the servant is worthy of his hire.
In my opinion, with the tremendous yields in taxes from Mr. Benson's tax reforms, more money should be poured into industry that is manpower oriented so as to produce jobs quickly. More money should be poured into research to develop our raw resources and manufacture new products. We should do far more processing in Canada of our own goods. At the present time over 60 per cent of our exports are of raw materials or are only partly processed, which I think is a disgrace. A little less than 40 per cent of the goods we sell are processed. Some 50 per cent of the value of the products that we produce are exported, while two-thirds of our imports are processed.
The labour content of a processed article is three times that of a raw resource product. This indicates the necessity for tax cuts and for the stimulation of the manufacturing sector. This fact strikes home when we realize that Canada has over 600,000 people unemployed out of a population of 22 million and a work force of around eight million. We have the greatest known amount of raw resources per capita in the world, yet we have the highest unemployment rate in the developed world. I say that without criticism but with a good deal of sadness. There are nearly 80,000 jobs in Canada that cannot be filled because there is no one to fill them, yet Ottawa spends $2 billion a year on benefits to the unemployed. What a way to run a country. We have manpower centres for training people and we have unemployment offices; nevertheless, in face of the stark facts we must point the finger at the inability of the government to solve our problems. The socialists say that they would cure the trouble. They would probably adopt the Swedish method-work or starve and this is not acceptable to a free society.

look at us, they acknowledge us, they even smile to attract our attention and sympathy, there is no doubt about that.
Mr. Speaker, the budget really reflects that change of attitude from a majority to a minority government composed of almost the same men, the same ministers and the same Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).
In his speech, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) told us strongly that the budget would result in creating more than 300,000 new jobs, that the LIP projects would be more fully and more easily subsidized than before. In my opinion, the budget as it was tabled, even with the pension increases and the tax reductions of around 5 per cent, will not create a single additional job in Canada.
It does not promote industry either. I shall give a striking example. The hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Pelletier), a riding which I well know, talked about his region. I did not have the pleasure of hearing him but, last February 22 he talked about the unemployment problem and the economic doldrums in his riding; it is not the only one in that position. The riding of Saint-Hyacinthe encounters difficulties in the same areas, what with economic stagnation and now hopes raised in the budget of the hon. Minister of Finance.
There is a good reason to hope that Sherbrooke will become again the prosperous queen of the Eastern Townships. The hon. member for Sherbrooke emphasized the situation of unemployment and distress in his riding and this is still true after more than ten years of continuing Liberal administration. If things are going badly in Sherbrooke, in Quebec and throughout Canada, with regard to the economy, the Creditistes are not to be blamed because it is the Liberals who are running the government. They laughed at the Creditistes when we offered solutions. When we made suggestions to the government, they found that funny but here is a Liberal member who complains that the Liberal riding of Sherbrooke is in distress. The Creditistes do not run the government, they do not administer the Canadian economy nor are they responsible for unemployment, low wages and distress which exist in Canada and in Sherbrooke in particular.
As I found it from reading Hansard at page 1561, here is what the hon. member for Sherbrooke said:
From 1965 to 1972, employment in the manufacturing sector in Quebec rose by 7.4 per cent, while it dropped by 10.8 per cent in Sherbrooke.
I think that in Drummondville, in Saint-Hyacinthe, in those parts of the Eastern Townships, the problem is about the same.
Therefore, if the manufacturing sector is important, our region is becoming a marginal area-
It is the hon. member for Sherbrooke who is speaking.
-and we can prove, in the light of valuable information that the city of Sherbrooke can in no way expect to have an economic recovery without substantial grants from the federal government.
At that time, the citizens or the industries in Sherbrooke will be called corporate welfare bums because the government will help them or will try to help them. The hon. member for Sherbrooke has complained saying that industrial structures were lacking, that the wages paid in Sherbrooke were below those paid elsewhere in Canada in the garment industry.

The unemployment rate varies from 11.6 to 11.8 per cent in Sherbrooke, while 20 to 25 per cent of the people in the Eastern Townships live in poverty. That is what the hon. member for Sherbrooke says.
But whose fault is it, Mr. Speaker? Who is to be held responsible for unemployment in Sherbrooke or elsewhere? Whose fault is it if wages paid in Sherbrooke are lower than the national average? Whose fault is it if plants in Sherbrooke leave this town to go to Ontario?
A plant closes down because of imports in the area of footwear, for instance. The manufacturer blames the government for not taking the necessary steps to help Canadian workers.
I have here a letter dated February 2 that was sent by the Kaufman Footwear Company Limited in Sherbrooke to its employees. The government is in office. What does management say?
Due to the economic situation, the company deemed necessary to stop production in Sherbrooke.
The decision to close down was based on the fact that the plant is in a non-competitive position mainly as a result of footwear imported from countries where wages are very low.
Italy, Czechoslovakia, Japan are countries which sell footwear in our country. Mr. Speaker, here are statistics related to the import of footwear of all kinds during the first 11 months of 1972. Manufacturers are right to complain about imports. From the countries I just mentioned, 47,117,826 pairs of shoes have been imported. The people from these countries manufacture footwear at a cheap cost because salaries there are not high.
Mr. Speaker, the material is less expensive than in Canada and the Canadian government allows the import of 47 million pairs of shoes so that industries like Kaufman Footwear Limited are obliged to close down. I have before me a letter from which I shall quote an excerpt:
Many attempts to create new lines such as boots for ladies and shoes for men, have not succeeded in producing the number of additional pairs needed by the plant to increase its productivity. The government has heard the representations made by shoe manufacturers with regard to the situation of the footwear industry, but it does not want to "listen" and take corrective measures which would help the Canadian workers in the footwear industry.
It should be clearly understood that the recent demand of employees for representation is not the reason which has brought about the above-mentioned decision.
The production will continue until or about May 4, 1973. A committee will be set up to help you, if possible, find jobs in other places. If there are employees who are interested to be sent else-wherere-
But in other places, measures are taken to reduce employment. After 25, 30 or 40 years of employment, in Sherbrooke city, how could workers consider being moved to other places like Matagami, for example? Workers are told to go to James Bay to face an intolerable situation in Canada. The company says and I quote:
If there are employees who are interested in being employed elsewhere, they should speak to their foreman so that the necessary information could be directed to the responsible persons.
We regret that this is the only course available to us. Your cooperation through the years has been appreciated.
February 27, 1973

Here is a situation where 300 workers are losing their jobs, while the minister says in his budget speech: We will create 300,000 new jobs in Canada. What a joke! On the other hand, the minister of Finance said: We will present a budget which will create employment and after two or three weeks, or after the budget speech, manufactures and mines are closing up in my region as well as elsewhere. An exclusive control over the dairy industry is being set up in the province of Quebec because small industries cannot operate with profit. Therefore large organizations buy the small dairy operations to gain control over that industry throughout the province of Quebec. Yet no one hears about that. The "big people" who buy do not say a word and the small businessmen who sell are appointed directors of a new plant that is set up to control exclusively the production and distribution of dairy products in our province.
That happens in a particular sector of the economic activity. But the budget will not create a single job, and I am deeply convinced of that even if the old age pensions are increased to $100 a month as we have been urging for many years. We advocated the payment of the old age pension at 60, the same pension for the spouse, but the government does not take that into account. Today, all hon. members know that a 60 year old man cannot find a job because there is no place for him in our society. And the government does not do anything to help her.
In the field of initiatives, the government thought it would have more money for the LIP program, money that would be earmarked for worthwhile projects from municipalities or intermediate organizations. But they say now: We are getting too many applications. They have paid for ads in the newspapers, on the radio, in all media telling people: Quick! Send in your local initiative or opportunities for youth projects. They have received
30,000	projects, they approved 7,000 so that leaves 23,000 citizens or groups who are not treated fairly, even though they have submitted worthwhile projects. Again, they are laughing at people when they pay advertisements to tell them: Submit your projects quickly and we shall approve them. Everyday, they turn down local or municipal initiatives projects from young as well as not so young people.
Mr. Speaker, we have also asked for assistance for university and CEGEP students. A kind of salary for students, they think that it is funny. Why are the young people on strike in universities? Because they are not learning French? Because they are learning too much English? Because they cannot pay for their tuition fees!

If a war broke out, the government would find the means to finance the studies of all those students who are striking in Montreal, in military colleges or universities and in such a case we would not call this aid anticipated salaries but a pay which would enable them to pursue studies paid for by the government.
Mr. Speaker, if, in wartime, it is possible to help young people of 18, 19 or 20, there is no one valid reason in the world for not helping them in peacetime in order to prevent them from sinking into disorder and helter-skelter as it is presently the case at the University of Montreal and at the University of Quebec in Montreal.
Mr. Speaker, there are limits to preposterousness and it is economic preposterousness to bring forward a budget which aims at distributing crumbs to the population on the whole. We will go on suggesting to and asking the government to entertain broader views. They have broad views when it comes to paying the interest on the public debt; the budget of the Minister of Finance will increase the public debt by $21 billion or $3 billion in interests only. The hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) said recently we should have increased that debt by $4 billion or perhaps $5 billion. We say that instead of going into debt with figure makers, we should use the Bank of Canada. Let us have its new governor write the figures which are necessary to the normal development of a country like ours. Then Mr. Speaker, we would be able to bring in a progressive budget, a budget of initiatives, in short a budget which would really serve the superior interests of the Canadian nation.

Mr. Speaker, I am particularly pleased to take part in the debate on the budget and to express my satisfaction on behalf on my constituents concerning the measures proposed by the minister to fight unemployment and to reduce taxes for the middle class and the low-income group. I was particularly pleased to see that the old age security pension and the veterans pension were to be increased.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) brought in a realistic budget which aims at controlling inflation and fight-
