mg unemployment. He even specifies that 300,000 new jobs will be created. This is auspicious and likely to give confidence again to manufacturers and businessmen. We rely on their investments to create new jobs.
Mr. Speaker, a great portion of my riding is industrial: Boucherville, Saint-Bruno and Saint-Hubert, Chambly and Beloeil have well organized industrial parks. For example, Boucherville, Saint-Bruno and Saint-Hubert have agreed to take advantage of the new facilities offered by Quebec Industry and Commerce Minister Saint-Pierre who made funds available to them to help pay qualified commissioners and to interest other industries in settling in the area.
The Department of Regional Economic Expansion paid to date several million dollars in my riding and I recently heard the new incumbent of this department (Mr. Jamieson) say that a review of those programs would be made and that even more substantial benefits would be granted to small and large industries.
In another part of my riding, we find heavy industries. Mr. Speaker, this could be the Canadian Ruhr if only the government accepted to build deep water wharves on the south shore at Varennes and Contrecoeur. I made representations to have some of the Montreal harbour facilities moved to the south shore but without result. The officials talk nonsense. One day they say yes, the other they say no, and discussions have been going on for 15 years. I am fed up with those stupidities. I urge the minister to approve the establishment of industries such as Gulf Oil Limited in Varennes and others such as The Steel Co. of Canada Ltd. and Dosco Steel Division, Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation Limited in Contrecoeur, that employ thousands of people. We must act.
Mr. Speaker, the economy of the south shore, and especially of my constituency, is at stake. Several heavy industries lack only the permission to go ahead with planned expansion. Branches are planned at Varennes and Contrecoeur. Heavy industry naturally covets this site, and the construction of wharves there is of the first importance.
I suggest that we do without the intermediary of the Port of Montreal, which has too many problems to face. I again call on the minister to study this situation so that a decision may be taken without further delay, for unless it is, the south shore will continue to be an underprivileged area.
I was pleased that the Speech from the Throne mentioned that the question of feed grain would be dealt with in this session. Bravo! The dairy industry, too, should continue to benefit from a dynamic policy, so that farmers may be assured of a just and equitable income.
I should like also to congratulate the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford), who is responsible for the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, on having made it possible for more young and not-so-young people to have their own homes and to move to my constituency, which is the natural dormitory for the city of Montreal.
There is some amazing development going on in my area. Serious promoters and contractors are helping to develop this small stretch of land that has become a

marvellous place thanks to the new facilities I mentioned just now.
In my constituency, there is also a part of the Chambly canal which, since last June, has been transferred from the jurisdiction of the Minister of Transport to that of the National Parks Branch of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. Built over a century ago, this canal is in an appalling condition besides harming considerably the normal evolution of the Chambly area. The obsolete bridges built for horse-driven carriages should have been replaced years ago to conform with minimum standards acceptable to modern traffic.
The construction of a detour to the highway at present closed to traffic has become necessary on account of the canal. The Richelieu River, which hit critical levels for the last three years, threatens to create a situation which could prove catastrophic this spring. And despite those urgent needs, among so many others, various papers in this country have been literally shocked at the sight of the credits granted Quebec by the federal government.
I do not want favours for the Chambly constituency, but only that works which have been delayed for too long and which are absolutely necessary be carried out if this area is to achieve normal economic development.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I urge the responsible minister to make a list of the credits voted for the Canadian canal system. He will see that Chambly canal over 20 years has received only poor grants compared with the Trent and Rideau canals. Chambly, a historical site because of its fort and its monuments, has a particular touristic role to play. In fact, the American people coming from New York take the canal, stop at the Chambly marina, follow the Richelieu river to Beloeil where, again, a marina is to be found. Those marinas probably have benefited from help, for the tourist industry is necessary and has importance for our country. And that magnificent district could benefit from help given those marinas. But up to now, they are the concern of benevolent organizations still at work, but which should not be discoui'aged, because they do care for the valuable aid they could obtain and that could benefit the whole area.
I hope that the minister will seriously consider these requests. He can be sure that I will renew my requests in order to get justice for that region.
Presently a study jointly conducted by the federal and provincial governments aims at cleaning the Richelieu river and at the diversion into that river of the Chambly canal, which I mentioned a while ago, where old bridges are on the verge of falling down. However that study is proceeding at a snail's pace. Three provincial and three federal engineers are carrying out that study. I recently heard that two were going to resign to take up new positions. In my opinion, the task should be entrusted to an independent study group, the matter being so important that decisions should be taken without delay to do justice to that area which experiences troubles and problems and I am asking the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) and the Quebec government to resume that study after having entrusted it to an independent organization.

Mr. Speaker, all the demands are surely timely because I have been interested in public administration for over 28 years. I was elected to work constructively with a party and a team which I trust and support. However, we must take into consideration the claims and difficulties of which the government is probably unaware. I do not wish to speak about my background, but I have examined those problems and I would like some assistance to solve them in the interests of my constituents.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak for the first time in this House and I hasten to join other hon. members in congratulating Mr. Speaker on his re-appointment as well as Mr. Deputy Speaker on his appointment. Other hon. members have spoken in glowing terms of their past association with Mr. Speaker. I cannot do that, inasmuch as I did not know Your Honour until a few weeks ago, but I have come to respect the Chair and admire the many capabilities of its occupants.
As I make my contribution to this budget debate, I will propose some radical changes which, I believe, have not been heard in this House previously. I shall develop a case for the elimination of taxes on personal incomes and the substitution of a tax on personal spending.
But first, I would like to say that I have observed another tradition in the House, which is to include in a maiden speech a detailed account of one's own riding. If I say that I have been pleased to have lived there for 17 years, that should say quite a lot about Vancouver Quadra. However, it may be helpful to what I am going to say to explain that Vancouver Quadra is probably a choice example of an urban residential riding. Vancouver Quadra stretches two thirds of the way across the centre of the city of Vancouver. It is eight miles from end to end, and varies in depth from one and a half to two and a half miles. It is the only riding in Vancouver that has boundaries in common with each of the four other ridings in the city. It contains no industry; the commercial areas are principally neighbourhood oriented; and there is not a single major shopping centre.
Although Vancouver Quadra is quite different from some rural ridings with their enormous distances, and from some of the high rise ridings of the big cities, the residential cross-section is complete. We have new high rise apartments and ancient walk ups. We have luxurious stone mansions and modest frame cottages. We have the university residences, low income housing, old folks homes, an army base, and even a youth hostel. These buildings are all called "home" by their occupants-the people, the families who live in Vancouver Quadra.
These are the families that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) has overlooked in his budget. Yet, he said he had produced a family budget. Now, Mr. Speaker, the minister is a smooth talker and is well known for this quality. He may have been able to smooth over the rough spots, and the morning after budget night it is possible that many families thought the minister was truly their knight in shining armour.
I am sure that nobody on this side of the House, least of all the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield),
The Budget-Mr. Bill Clarke
would condemn the budget in total. Our leader has been trying to sell this package to the government for years. Just think of his policies on the issues of tax cuts, pensions, and unemployment. But by now the analysts have had a chance to dig deeper into Turner's maze, and the media are telling the whole story. In short, as one editorial put it, there is less to it than meets the eye at first glance.
I will not repeat the words of previous speakers on this side of the House except to say that the people in Vancouver Quadra are now aware that the budget lacks the incentives to business which would ease the unemployment problem; lacks incentives to Canadians to invest in Canadian business; and lacks policies to combat inflation. They have heard that a Conservative government would have gone full speed on expansion of the economy and would have introduced temporary controls on prices and incomes. This is what the voters in Vancouver Quadra said they wanted last October 30.
There are no farms in my riding, Mr. Speaker, but the residents of Vancouver Quadra have had a chance to wonder why the family owners of small businesses should be less entitled to pass them on free of capital gains tax than should the family owners of farms. The government's policy of discrimination was undoubtedly arbitrarily political. It has no basis in logic. But my constituents have been disappointed in Liberal budgets before, and they have been disappointed in the Liberal government for years. They can recall the early days of tax reform when the government said that the primary aims of tax reform were equity and simplicity. They know that the Liberals have given us neither.
My constituents have been frightened and confused by white papers. They have seen business decisions postponed because of uncertainty about taxation. There is no telling how much unemployment can be attributed directly to this uncertainty. It is an accepted fact that businessmen will work under any given set of rules, but it is an equally well accepted fact that the one thing that businessmen cannot tolerate is uncertainty about those rules. When businessmen are faced with uncertainty about the rules they pull back on the reins and, as a result, there is a general slowdown of business activity. This slowdown costs jobs. Some of my friends at home have given up waiting for the government to untangle the tax mess. They cannot understand the new tax law themselves, so they go to some of my fellow chartered accountants who are in the tax advisory business. These professional tax advisers are unable to give any more than the most basic advice on taxation, in spite of the fact that some of them have done little but study the government's tax reform for years.
The minister had a chance truly to reform his predecessor's so-called tax reform, which has been so justly criticized, but the only reform this budget contains is the removal of one arbitrary restriction on small businesses. Now, they can invest their surplus funds in other Canadian companies on terms equal to those granted to foreign investors. Wasn't that a nice gift? After the Minister of Finance takes away the whole loaf, Mr. Speaker, he expects people to appreciate it when he gives back the crumbs.

February 27, 1973
The Budget-Mr. Bill Clarke
The real test of the budget is yet to come. The government says it got the message on October 30 of last year. Well, Mr. Speaker, just wait until after April 30 this year, after the taxpayer has had to wrestle with the new simplified tax return, complete with schedules in glorious colour. Then, the government will get a real message from the voters. What we really need, in addition to the policies we have heard from my colleagues, is some real tax reform with simplicity and equity.
I would like to ask hon. members to reflect for a moment on the origin of income tax. Most of the members were not even born 56 years ago, and certainly only a very few could remember that horrifying day in 1917 when the government of Canada first imposed a tax on incomes. Of course, it was a temporary measure, its purpose being merely to cover the costs of the Great War. In fact, Mr. Speaker, until 1949 when we had a major revision of the tax law it was known at the Income War Tax Act. Now, we have the distinction of paying 10,000 civil servants to see that we pay the proper amount of income tax. The estimated cost of operating the Income Tax Department for the coming year is $153 million, nearly five times as much as the cost of operating the whole House of Commons for the same period.
In addition to that, the people of Canada must bear the cost of legal and accounting assistance to help determine what amount of income is considered taxable, and to advise us of the tax consequences of our every move. Bitter disputes are commonplace, and invasion of privacy becomes ever more frequent. So much for simplicity, Mr. Speaker.
Now let us have a look at equity. The present system is often thought of as being a tax on the rich. If one thinks about it, one can see that the rich man cares little about rates of tax on incomes. The income tax does not tax his wealth. Income tax is a tax, not on the rich but on the poor who are willing to work hard to become rich. Income tax is a disincentive. It discourages hard working and able Canadians from their good endeavours, and even has caused some of them to leave the country taking their labour, capital and initiative with them. We have a strange tax system, Mr. Speaker. Instead of taxing what a person takes out of the economy in consumption we tax what a person puts into the economy. We tax labour, by wages and salaries tax, we tax savings by tax on investment income; we tax initiative by capital gains tax.
Surely a more equitable measure of ability to pay tax is what a person takes out of the economy in consumption. If the amount of consumption were taxed, the result would be the equitable situation of everyone paying in direct proportion to his material standard of living. What could be fairer? A man would not be penalized for doing well and saving his money. Young people would find it very much easier to save up for furniture or a house. Such a system would have the added advantage of simplicity, and gone would be the annual tax nightmare. Gone would be the huge government police force, and gone would be the endless arguments about the amount subject to tax. This system of taxation was thoroughly discussed in a 1955 book by Nicholas Kaldor, a noted British economist and adviser to the British Labour Party.
There is also a precedent for this idea in this country. Already the government allows individuals to save up to $4,000 per annum tax free in a registered retirement savings plan. This money is taxed when it is taken out of the plan and spent, usually after the taxpayer has retired. Look at the effect of this idea on a young family starting out-and much is said about the difficulties facing them. At present, two young people working side by side to make a start for their family are forced to pay a vast portion of their income in tax, even though their consumer expenditures are very low. My suggestion would allow them to get a boost by paying a tax only on the amount they spend. Similarly, those on low incomes would pay little in tax, and high living Canadians would pay their fair share based on their high expenditures.
It may be said that such a system would be regressive. Well, Mr. Speaker, if it is the desire of any government to have equity and simplicity in a tax system it should be obvious that the existing system has so many faults that it is incapable of reform. In that regard, I should observe that it has a great similarity to the government of the day. So, Mr. Speaker, I say that 56 years of experience with a patched up system that taxes incomes has been a flop. I advocate the elimination of personal income taxes, together with all the problems and faults that have come along with such taxes since 1917. I encourage in-put to our society by freedom from tax, and recommend the institution of a tax on expenditure or consumption.

speakeroldname: Mr. Leonard Hopkins (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister oi National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) upon bringing in what in fact is a typical Liberal budget. In addition to the increases for old age pensioners and veterans, and the reduction of taxes generally, I express to him and to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) our appreciation in rural Ontario for the removal of the capital gains tax on the family farm. I also observe with great satisfaction that we are to have a considerable increase in expenditures for the Department of National Defence, to the tune of $236 million, which is approximately a 12) per cent increase.
I would like first to draw attention to the National Capital Commission. Our country is rich in history, and particularly in local history. We have not and do not put the kind of emphasis on our past that the people of pioneer days deserve. For example, the names of the counties clasped in the V of the Ottawa and St. Lawrence Rivers- Stormont, Dundas and Glengarry-ring like the echoes of an old hunting horn. Here the Macdonells, disbanded from the Royal Regiment of New York, were first in occupation. Other Scots followed and established the same tightly knit communities as in their native highlands. They adopted the routines of their French-Canadi-an neighbours, serving their land from May to October and going into the lumber camps for the rest of the year. By the 1860's, there were men of substance among them, and timber had become their business, so that they were acutely conscious of the receding forest. Their eyes were on the Ottawa valley where magnificent stands abounded, but this area was in fee to Montreal by virtue of the river route. Hence, their thoughts turned to railways and the possibility of a local line which would link up with the
[Mr. Clarke.l
February 27, 1973

systems of New England, whose markets clamoured for Canadian lumber.
The value of railways was exemplified during the Fenian invasion of the Niagara Peninsula on May 1, 1866. F. W. Cumberland, General Manager of the Northern Railway, received orders to concentrate the militia to meet the enemy; within 24 hours he had delivered 1,240 men at the threatened point, and twice that number were on their way. The invasion was over before it had begun. Perhaps we can say, Mr. Speaker, that Mobile Command is something that was not born just yesterday. Therefore, security, the profit motive and the status symbol of the railway business made this an attractive business to men of energy and ambition.
In the years immediately following 1871, a series of railways were built between Montreal and Ottawa. In 1879, a man by the name of J. R. Booth who was born in 1826 at Waterloo in the eastern townships came on the scene. At an early age he had learned the routines of railway construction in Vermont. In 1852 he arrived at Hull as helper in the construction of a sawmill; within a matter of months he was in the timber business for himself. From an initial venture at Chaudiere Falls, his interests rapidly spread until he owned 7,000 square miles of timber limits in the Ottawa valley as well as substantial holdings in other parts of the province. He was among the first to develop his own sales organization in the United States and his press for business grew beyond the capacity of the water route to Montreal. Hence, he was advised by his personal expert to go into the railroad business to transport his timber and lumber to market. He formed the Canada Atlantic Railway Company along with his partners William Perley of Ottawa and G. C. Noble of St. Albans.
On September 13, 1882 the first train steamed into the capital from Coteau Landing on the St. Lawrence. The Canada Atlantic succeeded from the start. What had begun as a timber carrier quickly became a general purpose railway traversing a wealthy area. A western extension along the Ottawa valley which would serve not only the Booth mills but the growing market towns, Arnprior, Renfrew and Pembroke, grew necessary. Beyond these settlements a vast expanse of merchantable forest awaited exploitation, and this necessitated the building of a new railroad up the Ottawa valley.
On March 24, 1888 the Ottawa, Arnprior and Renfrew Railway Company was incorporated to build the first 55 miles westward from the Canadian capital. Six weeks later, the Ottawa and Parry Sound Railway Company was entrusted with the construction of 157 miles between Renfrew and Scotia, on the Toronto-Callander branch of the Grand Trunk. The two companies were merged as the Ottawa, Arnprior and Parry Sound Railway. Construction began immediately in both directions from Renfrew to be completed in the following stages: Ottawa-Arnprior, 38 miles, opened May, 1893; Arnprior-Madawaska Junction, 93 miles, opened September, 1894; Madawaska Junction-Cache Lake, 36 miles, opened May 1895; and Cache Lake-Scotia, 46 miles, opened December 1, 1896. This was perhaps the first railway of any importance to be both financed and built by Canadians. At times 2,000 men were
The Budget-Mr. Hopkins
at work; the roadbed rose and the steel went down with the swing and precision which were the hallmarks of the Booth enterprises.
On October 5, 1896 the J. R. Booth group took over and completed the Parry Sound Colonization Railway between Scotia and Parry Sound. Another subsidiary, the Pembroke Southern Railway Company built 21 miles of track to join the town of Pembroke with the Canada Atlantic at Golden Lake, 88 miles west of Ottawa. This project cost $264,500 of which $139,500 represented federal, provincial and municipal subsidies. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we can readily assume that regional development programs did not start yesterday.
At one stage a passenger could buy a ticket at the town of Renfrew for 75 cents and receive not only a round trip ticket for 117 miles of travel, but also a 50 cent seat at the Ottawa Opera House. The J. R. Booth railways eventually ended up in the CNR system; and today the line is still in operation from Ottawa to Arnprior, Renfrew, Eganville, Golden Lake, Wilno, Barry's Bay, Madawaska and Whitney on the edge of Algonguin Park.
It is my proposal to the national capital commission that a passenger train for tourist traffic could be developed as a great attraction, because all these places in the Ottawa valley and the Madawaska valley as well as the timber resources of that area have played such a major role in the area history and economic life of our national capital of Ottawa. Tourists visiting Ottawa could travel to Algonquin Park on a train that should be modelled after those of the pioneer days. We might even bring back the so-called old-fashioned steamer and the pot bellied stove in the coach if the Minister of the Environment would permit it, Mr. Speaker. Not only would the train ride be of an original nature for the tourist traffic, but passengers would be free to get off at any community along the line to play golf, go fishing, water ski, to stay at a resort area for a day or a week, or to go skiing, skidooing at Mount Madawaska at Barry's Bay, or go on hikes through Algonquin Park. Other forms of attraction would be limitless, including the natural beauty and history of the region. The old station buildings along the way could be rejuvenated or rebuilt, to serve as entertainment centres as well as places to purchase tickets; though I doubt very much if they could purchase a ticket for the National Arts Centre for 50 cents. Not only would this be an added attraction for Ottawa as a capital city, but it would bring back the prominent economic relationship between the valley and our nation's capital.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, I make this proposal in all seriousness because we, as Canadians, have a habit of destroying those things of our past history rather than preserving and promoting them. Therefore, I call upon the National Capital Commission, the various historical societies up and down the valley, to back this project before it is too late and the rail line is destroyed in the name of progress, hence destroying one of the most romantic symbols of Ottawa valley history. May I also appeal through you, Mr. Speaker, to Ottawa City Council to back this proposal so that relationships between Ottawa and its valley communities will prove of great value to all concerned.

February 27, 1973
The Budget-Mr. Hopkins
Mr. Speaker, I should now like to go on to another item of primary importance to me and every Canadian, that is the increase in the defence budget of 121 per cent, something that is not only needed in order to take the strain off many areas of departmental personnel at this time, but is also necessary if we are going to keep pace with modern equipment, training and everyday demands on the members of our armed forces. We do hear complaints about the spending estimates of the Department of National Defence from time to time but this, I believe, is basically because the critics, who intend to be sincere in their comments, really do not fully realize the extent and depth of the operations, the demands and the expertise of the men and women in the forces. Fortunately, most people do fully understand their impact on Canada and the world at large.
Historically, the Canadian forces have pioneered in virtually every major field necessary for getting into the Arctic, living there and working in the extreme climatic conditions. Most of the airfields and airstrips which are now under the Department of Transport or civilian jurisdiction were started by military forces. The fear of the Arctic which was a major drawback to any northern venture before the Second World War, was largely overcome by the presence of the search and rescue organization of the forces. If people know that the government is going to look for them if they are lost or forced down, the fear of non-survival is substantially reduced.
In the post-war period, when the Royal Canadian Air Force was photographing the whole of Canada, their operations took them into every corner of the high Arctic. The maps which resulted from these efforts made navigation possible. New techniques for air navigation were worked out by the forces, which were adopted by the United States Air Force and civil operators and provided for accurate air travel where the magnetic compass was useless. At the same time, army ground survey parties were adding to the knowledge and topography of Canada with new data for maps and a mapping section.
The army, too, for nearly 20 years maintained the Northwest Highway system.
The navy pushed the first large ship, the icebreaker HMCS Labrador, through the northwest passage, showing the way for future commercial ventures.
Communications in those early days were primitive. From 1946 to 1964, the forces constructed and operated the Northwest Territories and Yukon radio system, which was finally taken over by CN Telecommunications. The DEW line, too, provides radio communications which up to now would have been economically impossible for small civil use but became more and more important to north-south communications for civilians.
As communications improved and airfields became available, as maps were produced, as navigation became possible, as fuel was available and as the fear of northern flying was dissipated, more and more civilians pushed north for a wide variety of reasons, many of them economic. This is only a short list of the major contributions made to northern development by Canadian forces.
I would like now to speak about the training of the Canadian forces and their preparation for tasking by the government in both their national and international roles.

The people of Canada and, I think, many members of this House, assume, and rightly assume, that the Canadian forces can do just about any job that is given to them. We assume that they have such training and such expertise in thousands of specialities that they can go into any environment, on land, on the sea or in the air, and do what we ask of them. In recent years we have asked them to fly into the middle of a shooting war between India and Pakistan, to pick up Canadian civilians. We have asked them to fly 4,000 miles south to earthquake-ravaged Peru on a humanitarian mission for Canada, and to operate off tiny airstrips high in the Andes evacuating the sick and the injured. We ask them to buck North Atlantic gales to rescue the crews of foundered vessels. We ask them to parachute into the scene of a crashed aircraft, with all the survival skills and medical knowledge necessary to save the crash victims. We have asked them to operate in the deserts of North Africa and in the heat of Yemen, in the jungles of the Congo and the mountains of the Himalayas for the United Nations. We have asked them to control and clean up a giant oil spill on the east coast of Canada. We have asked them to build six airfields in the high Arctic, to serve both civilian and military air traffic. We asked them to dive 2,000 feet into the sea in highly sophisticated submersibles and to take a good look at our Continental shelf. We have asked them to keep under constant surveillance the million and a half square miles that we designate as the Canadian north. And, most recently, we have asked them to assume the dangerous and delicate role of supervising the cease fire in Viet Nam.
These are just examples taken at random. But in each of these instances they have done what we asked of them without question, and with a skill and professionalism which has often drawn international praise. However, the variety of tasks that we give to our soldiers, sailors and airmen taxes them almost to the limit. All of this requires a lot of training to bring the new recruits up to the high standards required by the forces and to keep the old hands up-to-date with ever-expanding technology, a technology which is often reflected first in the vehicles and weapons of defence. That is why we need an increased defence allocation in the budget. This training requires a large and highly professional teaching and instructional staff. It needs schools and sophisticated training facilities and training aids. It needs-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, those of us who are privileged to sit in this House for the first time find ourselves caught in a set of unique circumstances, many which have had the effect of thrusting freshman members into the thick of the fray sooner than it has been customary. At least, that is the impression I get from some veteran members, Mr. Speaker. Speaking for myself, I have been struck by the excellence of some of the speeches given by some of my colleagues, on both sides of the House who, as I am, are sitting in the House for the first time. I am also impressed by the way the new men appear to be so eager to be involved in the business of the House and in committee work. If I may remain on that issue for another moment or two, I believe that my party in this House is fortunate in many respects. For one thing, we new members have an exceptionally talented and knowledgeable group of veteran members to lead us through the difficult days of learning our way around. In my view they have made it possible for us to become effective members in a shorter time than I would have expected.
As to the budget, Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to try to take this budget item by item and expose its deficiencies. This has been done most effectively by my leader and many of my colleagues. I understand that in budget debates a member can digress and dwell on issues that for him or her have a special meaning or interest. This is what I would like to do; and while I will not guarantee that all of my colleagues will agree with everything I say, I would be less than honest if I were to let that fact deter me from my course. To set the stage for my remarks, I would refer my colleagues to a statement made by the mover of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne on January 5, the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Blais). As recorded on page 25 of Hansard for that date he said:
I am sure that no member of this House was directed by his or her constituents to come to the House to squelch debate.
1 give the freshman member for Nipissing full marks for that observation, Mr. Speaker, but I cannot extend the same charity to the seconder of the Address in Reply to
The Budget-Mr. Mitges
the Speech from the Throne, the hon. member for Lachine (Mr. Blaker). As recorded on page 28 of Hansard for January 5, he said:
Many of us had thought that the great debate on Canadian unity
was over;-
What a statement that was, Mr. Speaker. I referred to those statements because I intend to speak for a few minutes on the question of national unity. National unity is one of the subjects closest to my heart, Mr. Speaker, and I will question some of the misconceptions that are presently being bandied about by some people for purely personal and partisan purposes.
In the first place, Mr. Speaker, no thinking person in Canada could accept the statement that the debate on national unity is over. The debate on national unity will continue long after those of us here have gone to a better or a worse place. I will refer to one more statement in Hansard before I continue. As recorded, on page 58 of Hansard for January 8, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said:
It is obvious, Mr. Speaker, that the question of national unity has not been solved in this country.
The Prime Minister should know that better than anyone, Mr. Speaker. During the terms of the last two governments, and especially during the term of the present government, the cause of national unity has deteriorated as at no other time in our history. Canadian voters tried to tell the Prime Minister just that on October 30 last year; and while he admits that that is so, I still do not believe that he or his government plan to alter their stand on the issue. There is great danger that too many people in Canada today will accept the view of the hon. member for Lachine, that we should not engage in any further dialogue on the question of unity. The hon. member must be afraid that his views on the subject will not stand scrutiny and he must be afraid that his views will not stand the test of dialogue.
After the recent election, the Prime Minister complained that there were members of this House who had used racism in their election campaigns; so far he has not yet named any names, and I doubt if he will. The Prime Minister has said, Mr. Speaker, that there will not be real unity in Canada until we in English Canada accept the fact that we are a bilingual country. We accepted that fact back in 1966; all of us accept that fact today. Yet, what do we see today? Almost daily on CBC television we see evidence that the Quebec separatist movement is growing as it has never grown before in our long history.
Whatever we are doing to achieve national unity and weld our people together in a common bond is not working. That is the main reason I believe we should undertake further study of the problem; and we should not be afraid of dialogue. It is when people do not talk about problems that the small problems develop into big problems. I do not mean the small, whimsical comments of the type characterized by the Prime Minister when he said that bilingualism will be a fact when a French Canadian can go to Vancouver and order a hamburger in French. This is not what the issue is about, but the trouble is that there have been too many people talking in just that way about a very serious problem.

February 27, 1973
The Budget-Mr. Mitges
I have read and heard, Mr. Speaker, that whenever anyone dared to stand up and ask questions about this subject, he was branded a bigot. If I worried about such things as that, Mr. Speaker, I would not be here. I happen to care a great deal about where we are going and I am concerned about what will happen to us if people continue to use the issues of race and language for political gain. In my case, I am a Canadian of Greek heritage. I am proud of my heritage, but I would not let it stand in my way of being a Canadian because that is exactly what I am. I do not want a hyphen in front of my name. I am not prepared to go along with anyone who proposes policies that will dilute or diminish the strength of Canadianism, not as an alternative but as a fundamental and basic philosophy.
Last Friday the Leader of the Opposition said in this House that we need in Canada an effective government, an honest government, a government that can be trusted. I cannot help feeling that that is at the root of most, if not all, of our problems in Canada today. We do indeed need honest government in Canada, a government that has the trust of the people, if we are to move forward and root out the real causes of dissent and disruption in our country. There is a group in Canada that professes to present the Canadian viewpoint, Mr. Speaker. They make a lot of noise, but they are not the answer. The Committee for an Independent Canada is not presenting or pushing the cause of Canadianism. They are anti-American, first and last, and that is negative. What I want to see is a government that will inspire people throughout our country to proclaim their Canadianism. I am a Canadian because I want to be, and in my view anyone who lives here and shares the bounty of Canada should be just as willing and anxious to say the same.
The Prime Minister keeps coming up with ad hoc policies designed to demonstrate his feeling for the different cultures in our country. Since money is no object to this government, he offers everyone and anyone money to do his or her thing. We do not need government assistance to divide our people into cultural segments. We need a government that will recognize the clear fact that the majority of the people in our country want to be recognized as Canadians and that everything else we want to do will be made easier if we take that logical step.
I hear that we must hurry and erect barriers here and there to preserve our cultures from exposure to other societies, such as that in the United States. People complain that we are becoming Americanized and that we must take action to reverse the situation. Again, Mr. Speaker, this is palpable nonsense. All the world is changing; people are changing and countries are changing. Anything that cannot stand up to exposure to other cultures and ideas is not worth saving. It would be working against natural forces, against nature itself, and it would mean that we would have to adopt a policy of isolation.
The only cultures, in my view, that we as Canadians must work to preserve in their pure form are the cultures of our native peoples, the Indians and Eskimos. Their cultures are distinct from any other on the continent and they should be preserved. These people differ in their viewpoints, in their living and work habits and in their approach to the whole process of living. In many cases

these people choose to move into the mainstream of Canadian life and so they will decide for themselves how much or how little of their native culture to keep. But, where people want to live in their own regions in a style of life different from our own, they must be encouraged and assisted. And, Mr. Speaker, they must be protected.
A final point on this subject might best be summed up by saying that our Canadian culture is only in danger of extinction if and when we admit that it is, and I do not admit that there is any real danger. As long as people talk openly and honestly about what they are, what they want to be and how this might be accomplished, there is no way that a small or even a large group of separatist rabble can accomplish the breakup of our country.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, each time I have the opportunity to rise in this House, I am always honored by the impressing attendance of my colleagues and this is most stimulating for me.
The budget speech of February 19 last is a new example of this government's concern about the individual's welfare and about those most in need. Indeed a host of measures announced in this speech are aimed at giving to the average Canadian and to the have-nots a more equitable share of our national resources through more generous tax cuts and for our pensioners notably increased pensions.
As underlined by the Minister of Finance himself (Mr. Turner), the objective of this budget is to reduce unemployment and inflation pressures, to eliminate the ill effects of past inflation, to increase take-home pay and to give to our senior citizens a more equitable share of our country's affluence so as to contribute to a balanced economic expansion throughout Canada.
No wonder this budget is welcome at all levels of our economy. The opposition finance critic, the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), having no serious criticism to make and dumbfounded as he was-and as everyone opposite was that night in the face of such an achievement by the Minister of Finance-merely criticized the minister and the government for borrowing from his party's platform, for having taken into account the needs of Canadians and for at last becoming aware of the situation of our senior citizens.
Who are those Conservatives to give lectures on the right of our senior citizens to government consideration when throughout the whole history of Sir John A. MacDonald's great party with their adulation or supposed adulation for our senior citizens, they barely managed to pay them $19 a month as compared with $82.88 and $155 which they now receive and $100 and $170 they will get starting April 1, 1973? They should be ashamed of such a meagre record. They are truly conservatives. To them this is not only a word, it is reality.
Instead of whimpering because, for instance, the minister announced a better formula than the one advocated by the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Stanfield) to
February 27, 1973

eliminate the erosion of the purchasing power caused by inflation and progressive taxation, he should have rejoiced. If the leader of the official opposition was serious, as I think he was when he made that suggestion, he should not recriminate because the Canadian citizen will have a better fate thanks to the beneficial action of this government. We would also have thought that the budget, which according to them is nothing but plagiarism, would not have prompted them to bring in a non-confidence motion. Since when, unless someone is off his rocker or marked by trappistine austerity, do we scourge ourselves and censure ourselves? It becomes more and more evident that the official opposition, its leader included, has only one purpose: Power at all costs. In the pursuit of that objective, whether the legislation is good or not, the main interest is to defeat the government.
I do not venture to claim that the budget will solve all the social and economic problems of today. Besides, what budget has ever performed such a feat? However, undeniably it will somewhat benefit the security and welfare of a great many Canadians. The economic consequences of increased old-age security pensions, veterans' allowances as well as substantial lowering of income tax, elimination of sales tax on some products and of customs duties on some goods cannot but bring great relief, particularly to lower income groups.
It is customary for the debate on the budget speech to provide an opportunity for hon. members to speak about their constituencies and the needs of their constituents. For the benefit of those who might not be over-familiar with the geography of the province of Quebec, I shall say that my constituency comprises two totally different areas. The first is the continental area-Bonaventure- located on the South-East coast of the Gaspe peninsula, north of Chaleur Bay and adjoining the province of New Brunswick. This area extends over more than 150 miles from East to West, and includes 38 localities, 30 of which are organized as municipalities. The second region comprises the Magdelen Islands, 150 miles from the coasts of the Gaspe peninsula, in the Gulf of St. Lawrence, covering an area of some 75 miles from East to West. These islands comprise 12 different localities, six of which are organized as rural municipalities. The population of the islands is close to 14,000 inhabitants, totalling, with Bonaventure, 56,700.
The main industries of these regions are fisheries, agriculture, forestry and tourism. In order to function as decently as possible and in a competitive way, they need increasingly easy access to foreign markets and to the major business centres. An adequate transportation system, at reasonable rates, is a primary necessity. Our fishermen and businessmen need modern harbour facilities, in keeping with their needs.
In so far as sea ports are concerned, there have been important improvements in the Magdalen Islands, as well as at Bonaventure, especially during the past years, although much remains to be done. For instance, the construction of the multipurpose harbour of Cap-aux-Meules is not yet completed. There has been proscratina-tion for over a year as to the site of an unloading docks for the ferry Manic. The construction of the fishing harbour at l'Etant-du-Nord was postponed because of last
The Budget-Mr. Bechard
year's delay in asking for tenders. I may say we are grateful to the minister directly on my right for obtaining this harbour last year.
Moreover, in order to retain a large number of fishermen in their industry, a suitable fishing harbour has been demanded for years in the Millerand area, more specifically in the municipality of Havre Aubert in the Magdalen Islands. Until now, we have been living on hope. It is essential that this work start this year if the number of welfare recipients is to be kept down, otherwise it would mean a further outlay of public funds. Entry Island has been retained as an unloading harbour. What has been done to date in order to improve conditions there other than letting the only wharf go to rot until fall, when a call for tenders will be made for long awaited repairs?
When one considers, Mr. Speaker, that this wharf is the only point from which the fish can be shipped to outside markets, and the only supply point for the island, one can easily wonder about the efficiency of our planners.
Still with regard to fishing, I am willing to recognize that there must be some centralization of our port facilities, for instance with regard to offshore fishing, in view, among other things, of the size of our modern fishing fleets and the fishing boats themselves. Such centralization results in better facilities for the fishermen, facilities better adapted to their needs. I am also willing to recognize that centralization for greater efficiency and better shelter is justified. However, I do not admit, and never will, that all the small harbours in the area should disappear, as has been the case in Bonaventure where over a distance of 100 miles, for instance, only three ports of harbours have been kept.
I sometimes wonder, Mr. Speaker, as you must also, what supergenius, what technocrat in need of publicity and, above all, promotion, wants to make sport of the fishermen by crossing out with a single stroke of his pen the facilities that are essential to fishing! As long as the sea produces lobster, there will be inshore fishermen. I wish the technocrats would understand that once and for all. The fisherman will therefore always need harbour facilities to bring in his catch and shelter his boat, unless the expert planners want us to go back to the mid 19th century, when the shore was often the only home port. Hippies develop in that direction!
Therefore, I call once more publicly for the development of harbour facilities for inshore fishermen from Port Daniel to Hopetown included, and especially in New Carlisle, in Bonaventure, in Ruisseau leBlanc which was favoured last year, in Caplan, as well as a proper maintenance of structures in March's Lane and Shigawake. Fishermen are calling for it and wish to retain their livelihood rather than to live on welfare, which they will be forced to do if we go on listening to some technocrat dreamers who issue their orders from the top of their ivory tower!
The economy growth of the whole Gaspe peninsula as well as the Magdalen Islands was seriously threatened in the past and still is today for lack of proper transportation means. Now that highway 6 is being rebuilt thanks to a Canada-Quebec agreement for the economic development of eastern Quebec (Lower St. Lawrence, Gaspe peninsula, Magdalen Islands), to which the federal government makes a financial contribution of 50 per cent, we should

February 27, 1973
The Budget-Mr. Bechard
develop an air transport policy. How many times did I say in this House that the Gaspe peninsula and my riding in particular had almost no air transport service at all? We are not less Canadians than others. I believe that it is no longer necessary for us to prove our devotion to the Canadian flag. But we should not be forever considered as simple-minded. Why should we be deprived of this basic modern link with other regions? We are calling for the setting up of a first class airline service for the Gaspe peninsula, on which passengers could rely because the carrier would keep to his schedule. Besides there is a splendid runway in Bonaventure, another one in Gaspe as well as in Havre-aux-Maisons, in the Magdalen Islands. The runway in Bonaventure, once improved and provided with the required instruments and facilities, could complete the network in our area. Why not develop it? With a little imagination, a first class service could pay for itself in our area. Subsidies, which are available elsewhere, would be just as welcomed in the Gaspe area, I believe. The mail which is so often delayed could come by air. Thus we could enjoy the same privileges or at least the same rights as those enjoyed by such remote areas as Newfoundland and British Columbia.
In the Islands, following numerous requests and representations of all kinds, the government created a roll on and roll off ferryboat service, operating between Prince Edward Island and Cap-aux-Meules, in the Magdalen Islands. While it is not the ideal solution, that ferryboat is a great improvement on what existed before. But what happened last summer clearly shows that it cannot fully meet the economic needs of the Magdalen Islands, especially with the increasing inflow of tourists in that beautiful area.
In addition, the trucks used for moving fish and perishables have a lot of difficulties finding room since they have no priority. It is urgent that this situation be corrected at least during the rush period between June and September. A parking lot should be provided on the Islands to relieve the approaches to the dock which are already overcrowded. The wharf I mentionned a while ago, intended for the ferry-boat, within the harbour should be built without delay in order to prevent unfortunate accidents. Because of the development of the tourist industry on the Islands, action should also be taken following the repeated requests for improving existing airport by extending the runways to give better access to larger aircrafts.
Since 1946, an interprovincial ferry service has been in operation between Dalhousie which is in the riding of the minister of Public Works (Mr. Dube), in New Brunswick, and Miguasha which is in the riding of Bonaventure in the province of Quebec. Subsidies have been payed up until now to the operator of that boat. However, at the close of last season, the agreement between the Canadian Transport Commission and the present operator having expired, in spite of the many representations made to both the previous minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) and the Canadian Transport Commission, the future of that ferry service is still very uncertain. I hope it is only an impression because our area would then be set back 30 years. I cannot believe that a population which has been
JMr. Bechard.]
neglected to such a point in the immediate past will be forgotten. If both levels of government develop a tourist industry by establishing a national park, tourist facilities and areas, they will be driving away those they want to attract by depriving them of an absolutely necessary link between the two provinces.
The role played by the Canadian National Railways, Mr. Chairman, is becoming very important for the economy of our area. There was a time not so long ago when railways were the only means of transportation. It cannot be said that all is well in the best of possible worlds, at present. For some time especially in our area we have been witnessing a kind of dance of death involving railway stations and station masters, cleverly orchestrated and directed by the authorities of this Crown corporation, for efficiency and economy reasons, as they say. I should like for my own information and for the information of my constituents to hear details on the savings that will follow from the replacement of the station master by a janitor paid on commission, in view of the rent that he will be paid for his accommodation and the fantastic number of long distance calls that will be necessary, compared with the salary now paid to the station master. This is pennywise and pound-foolish.
I wish to object once more to such an arbitrary and retrograde decision by the CNR in our area. Let me mention only one example. In Maria, Mr. Speaker, there is a hospital serving the community in a radius of more than 100 miles; it has a home for older people, one of the only medical clinics in the area, many dealers and businessmen; it is unthinkable that they should insist on depriving this community of a station master. Despite the very numerous representations made these past few years, I cannot understand this attitude and I hope that my message will reach the Canadian Transport Commission. I ask the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) to use his influence and to order this agency to revise its decision to accept the request of the Canadian National Railways. [English]

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is customary, on the occasion of a member's maiden speech, to extol at great length the virtues of one's own riding. Traditionally, this has made maiden speeches rather prolonged and often tedious affairs. However, I am privileged in being able to forgo this practice for I know of no prose, poem or song that can enhance or do aesthetic justice to the beauty of Winnipeg and Manitoba and the friendliness of our people.
Although words prevent me from expressing an accolade fitting to the true splendour of western Canada, I am sure the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), in view of his literary background and his party's showing in Manitoba on October 30, could recite some sort of verse for us. Let me assure him, though, that the ringing rhetoric of "fud-dle-duddle" will not suffice. Hopefully, the Prime Minister's new set of songwriters are more adept lyricists than his last.
I have the privilege of representing a constituency that for many years was represented by one of the most able and well respected parliamentarians of our time. I refer, of course, to the Hon. Gordon Churchill. My only hope is
February 27, 1973

that I, too, will be able to serve the people of Winnipeg South Centre, and Canada, in the same distinguished way.
The budget recently brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) is indicative of the manner in which the present government deals with problems. There is seldom any decisive leadership; rather, the government tends to meander along in a quandary until situations manifest themselves to such an extreme that action is unavoidable. Such is the case with the current budget. Some much needed proposals have been brought down, but only after the placing of great pressure upon the government from all sides, particularly the left.
The personal income tax cuts are a welcome measure, but this is a measure which has been long advocated by everyone, including the Economic Council of Canada. The $100 basic old age pension and the increase in veterans benefits are to be welcomed as beginnings. However, the government has proposed nothing to compensate these pensioners for the tremendous increase in food prices during the last year. Instead, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) maintains that Canadians should be happy with our food prices because compared with certain other countries our prices are relatively low. A budget which does not explain how a government is going to reduce the rate of increase in the cost of living is not good enough.
The government continues its wild spending spree. At the time of the last budget in May, the Minister of Finance called for expenditures of $16.5 billion, a 10 per cent increase over the previous year. Now the Treasury Board has asked parliament for an additional $1.8 billion to cover the government's spending obligations between now and the end of the fiscal year, March 31. This means that within a period of two years, federal spending has gone up from $13.2 billion to $18.34 billion, a 35 per cent increase. The government, however, appears to have no intention of arresting these growing expenditures. This is evidenced by the Minister of Finance's recent announcement that the government plans to spend a record $19.3 billion of taxpayers' money in the coming fiscal year.
The situation is such that Canada's GNP is growing less quickly than is the percentage being spent by government. In 1971 the total value of goods and services produced by the public was $67 billion. Of this, the government's revenue share was 37.7 per cent, almost 10 per cent higher than in 1961. During this ten-year period the government's role as a purchaser of goods and services from the private sector increased by nearly 300 per cent. In terms of money, this was an increase from $7.9 billion to $22 billion.
These are the facts. What they mean is that under the present government, Canada is being slowly steered toward increased state control of our lives. The government does not appear to have any intention of curbing its spending, especially with the possibility of an election at any time. Thus, a situation appears to exist which, if carried to its ultimate conclusion, will lead to a system of government capitalism instead of individual and private enterprise. This state capitalism would be the dominating unit in the economic system. It is obvious to me and my Progressive Conservative colleagues that something must be done to stop this ever-increasing government expenditure.
The Budget-Mr. McKenzie
One current government expenditure of particular concern to me is that of the federal bilingualism development program. Between January 1, 1970, and December 31, 1972, $167.8 million was spent on programs administered by the Secretary of State in an effort to implement various government bilingualism programs. I suggest that spending great amounts of money in an effort to implement the bilingualism program is an excellent idea, but only where a sufficient proportion of the population makes such an effort justifiable.
I do not believe that regions of Manitoba which have been designated as potential bilingual areas by the bilingual districts advisory board should be declared such. Like the Commissioner of Official Languages did in his second annual report, I question the need for and the negative effects of the establishment of bilingual districts outside the Ottawa region. The 10 per cent minority population rule used in designating bilingual districts is an arbitrary one. Furthermore, how are the lines on the maps to be redrawn? Will there be a redistribution of bilingual districts every ten years? There are numerous unanswered questions. I am in agreement with the commissioner when he suggests possibly abandoning the concept of districts altogether, instead of relying on strengthened interpretations of "significant demand" and "feasibility" as stated in the Official Languages Act to decide where bilingual government services should be provided.
lished so as to allay the fears of not only French-speaking Canadians but those of English-speaking western Canadians. Such a program might deal with the language problem by allowing the use of both languages in the federal civil service, but only in direct proportion to that particular language group's statistical number in the population. As it is now, the program does little but breed alienation in western Canada. It is also resulting in the unnecessary spending of millions of dollars.
The throne speech promised that in this session parliament will be asked to reaffirm the basic principles of bilingualism. In light of Mr. Spicer's comments and the tremendous expense being generated in efforts to implement the program, parliament would do well to re-examine not only the principles of bilingualism but their implementation. It is only by reviewing the effectiveness of the bilingualism program that parliament will find a fair and just solution satisfactory to both of Canada's founding peoples.
I have used the term "western alienation". This is a rather overworked term; none the less, it seems to accurately depict the feelings of discontent which characterize many Canadians. It is an honest feeling of westerners that they are not getting their share of the pie. Such feelings have been given substance by the actions of recent Liberal governments. In my riding of Winnipeg South Centre one particular government action more than any other is responsible for widespread feelings of dissatisfaction. I am speaking, of course, of the decision by Air Canada many years ago to move its overhaul base from Winnipeg in an effort to consolidate its overhaul functions in Dorval. Then, contrary to the promises made, the complete phasing-out of the Air Canada operation occurred.

February 27, 1973
The Budget-Mr. McKenzie
On April 3, 1969, the Minister of Transport announced that negotiations had been completed between CAE's parent firm, Northwest Industries, of Edmonton, and Air Canada for the sale of the Air Canada overhaul base. The Minister of Transport indicated that the federal government through its departments and agencies would lend strong support to the new enterprise. However, such has not been the case.
In mid-1969, CAE Aircraft signed a contract with the United States military through the Canadian Commercial Corporation which works for the Department of Supply and Services. The contract was to repair and overhaul military jet aircraft. This contract involved the direct employment of approximately 250 skilled workers. Suddenly, though, this T-39 contract was terminated. This, together with the Viscount phase-out, resulted in tremendously decreased employment.
A similar situation exists today. It is an urgent one. While the province has done what it can at the provincial level to assist CAE Aircraft, unless the federal government uses its resources to secure work for CAE it will be unable properly to maintain its operation. Lack of a viable air industry in Manitoba has resulted in great loss to the province in terms of expertise as all our skilled personnel leave to seek employment elsewhere.
Lay-offs in this industry are devastating. CAE is currently operating with skeleton crews. They have recently lost 17 more men, trained by Air Canada, who have gone to work at Dorval. Approximately 90 per cent of the aeronautical personnel, including engineers, consulting staff, supervisors and licensed mechanics, have been forced to move to Montreal. This is to say nothing of the expense of such a move. I have spoke to people who have been forced to move; they inform me of low morale amongst workers both at Dorval and CAE in Winnipeg. In both places there is much resentment of the government stemming from the government's failure to honour its many promises.
A great proportion of those who formerly worked at the Air Canada overhaul base in Winnipeg were constituents of Winnipeg South Centre, as are the bulk of those working for CAE Aircraft, its successor. The facilities and airports where men worked also are within my riding. Therefore I am concerned with the state of the aerospace industry in Manitoba. The aerospace industry held a special place in Manitoba's economy and the decision to transfer the base to Dorval dealt a serious blow to that economy.
The logic of the transfer escapes most people associated with the industry in Manitoba. Winnipeg should be the centre of a viable aerospace industry. Our geographical location, in the centre of North America, and proximity to the markets of the American mid-west are obvious reasons for the establishment of what could some day be a prosperous industry. At the time of the transfer to Dorval, definite promises were made by the Liberal government to do everything possible to maintain employment at the base and, if possible, to increase it. However, it appears that the government has little intention of honouring its commitment.
In order that hon. members may understand the situation, let me review it briefly. On November 22, 1963, Prime

Minister Pearson, as he then was, speaking in the House of Commons acknowledged the importance of the base to the economy of Winnipeg. He said:
For at least as far ahead as planning now extends, that is at least ten years, the Winnipeg facilities will continue to be used.
On June 5, 1964, in a letter to Mr. D. A. Thompson, Q.C., of Winnipeg, the then minister of transport in a letter to the Manitoba government assured Premier Roblin that every effort was being made to "maintain the level of Air Canada's activities in Winnipeg". On May 23, 1968, Prime Minister Trudeau wrote to Premier Weir of Manitoba stating:
You may be assured that the present government will honour the commitment made by my predecessor and that we will in addition vigourously search out alternatives aimed at maintaining a viable aircraft support industry in Manitoba.
Here are the remarks of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) on the air base being moved:
One of the worst decisions made in Canadian history.
He further stated:
No one endorses more strongly than I do the concept of decentralization of industrial activity.
Within the past fortnight the Prime Minister has visited Winnipeg. He has assured us that western interests are of equal importance to those of Quebec, that we must take the initiatives to press for their realization and that we must not passively wait government intervention. We will take him at his word. We believe in the importance of maintaining and promoting an air base in Winnipeg to serve central and western Canada. Winnipeg is the logical location. We believe that the Prime Minister should fulfil his promise to honour the commitment made to us by his predecessor to maintain a viable aircraft support industry in Manitoba.
We do not doubt the sincerity of the Minister of National Defence in his wish to serve western Canada, and we sympathize with the difficulties and restrictions he faces in this regard. But this issue is so essential to Winnipeg that we believe it is his responsibility to press for its realization. We believe that he should be prepared to resign from the cabinet and move to the back benches to challenge the Prime Minister's sincerity. Our cabinet representative should be expected to remind the Prime Minister of his advice and promise to us, and demonstrate that he stands by this principle. In my opinion, the Minister of National Defence has no other choice.
The people of Winnipeg South Centre remember these promises. They demand to know if the federal government recognizes its long-standing commitments to the aerospace industry in Manitoba. If the government does not recognize its commitments, then this feeling of alienation can only grow stronger not only in my constituency but among all the people of western Canada.
