subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it makes a difference to be addressing this House after rather than before supper. At least we have all returned replete with meat if not with wisdom.
I do not want to address myself to the specific points in the budget because so many of my fellow members in this party have addressed themselves to these points in particular. I could certainly tell the House what I like about the budget and what I dislike about it in terms of its particular elements, but I feel that in the past few days these elements have been adequately covered on both sides of the House.
My remarks will pertain to the budget: I will avoid making a travelogue about the beauties of Scarborough West. I know this is very difficult to resist, but I will manage to resist the temptation and will try to speak about the budget in general terms which are at least of interest to me and might be of interest to other members of the House.
First of all, it will not surprise members to my immediate right that I am prepared to congratulate the government on the budget. I think that the budget presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) is a kind of milestone for the parliament of Canada. Mind you, it is a retarded milestone because it is one that we should have passed many years ago. Nevertheless, it is rather nice to get to this particular milestone.
I should like to congratulate the Minister of Finance and the members of the government for returning to the age of Keynesian economics. We left them solidly behind three or four years ago, particularly in 1969 when in a fit of despair the government gave up trying to understand how to run an economy on the lines enjoined by Lord Key res and decided to go back to much more classical, indeed we could call them Victorian, procedures. The result of this kind of decision-making certainly caused an enormous amount of distress and pain across this nation. We all know now, including the government, that the policies adopted by the government some three years ago to fight what they thought was the great bugbear, namely inflation, simply brought about acute unemployment in this country and enormous distress to tens of thousands, indeed, hundreds of thousands of Canadians.
Therefore, I congratulate the government on having moved itself from the day before yesterday to yesterday so that now we are in a position to start talking about today. Now we are in a position to start talking about the problems that really face Canada, not the problems that the government then thought faced Canada. We are now in a position to start talking about the problems of this economy as an economy that is of the post-industrial age.
The Budget-Mr. Harney
Having congratulated the government, I must express a concern. I am not too sure that the government knows where it is going. I say this because there was so much left out of the budget and the address relating to the budget. For example, there was nothing in the budget or in the budget address about the spending and investment plans of those corporations which are directly owned or controlled by parliament. I refer to the Crown corporation in Canada. There was nothing, even in estimation or in prediction, about the spending and investment plans of the provincial governments or, indeed, of other levels of government in Canada. There was virtually nothing-just one sentence, I think-on possible monetary policy as it would apply in Canada in the coming year, and there was simply no attempt to try to ascertain what would be the plans and the position of the private sector in Canada.
The budget speech, in effect, was like a treasurer's report for a rather large bowling league. There was some talk about the cost of membership in the league. There was some talk about the benefits that would accrue from membership in the league and there was some talk of an annual banquet. But there was no attempt to try to understand what is really going on in the country. Can this House, then, know what is going on in the Canadian economy? Can it ascertain from the budget and from the address relating to it what will happen to the economy in the future? Is it possible for the government to be guiding the economy on the basis of so little consideration and so little information given to the House?
There was promise in the budget of tax cuts. We on this side, particularly in this corner of the House, welcome the provision for tax cuts. But at the same time, in the supplementary papers issued on budget night we were given a very clear indication that there would be no particular shift in the tax burden as the taxes applied to individual Canadians as opposed to corporations. For example, we are told in that supplementary document that last year some 44 per cent of all taxes received by the government came from individual contributions, and that this year some 44 per cent of taxes would come from the same sector; that last year some 15 per cent of our revenue came from corporations, and this year some 14 per cent would come from corporations-a decrease in taxes coming from the corporate sector. I am told that these projections include the effects of the bills that were to have been passed following the budget of May 8 last.
I want to tell the members of the government that if these projections are actually carried out through the implementation of corporate tax cuts, we will have achieved nothing in terms of real redistribution of the tax burden in this country and I and many others in this party will not stand for that kind of shell game. It is very obvious, upon any close analysis of the budget, that the only meaningful way in which the budget can have a beneficial effect on the average Canadian is to have personal income tax cuts and no corporate tax cuts, because it will be apparent to most Canadians that the tax cuts proposed by the Finance Minister a week ago last Monday will be totally ineffectual if the bills emanating from the May 8 budget are brought in.

February 27, 1973
The Budget-Mr. Harney
I have another reason for congratulating the Minister of Finance. I do not know whether he really deserves it. At any rate, he seemed to go all out for a policy of budgetary expansion. What I am going to say may sound a little heretical, Mr. Speaker, but heretical things have been said before from this corner of the House. It has become very obvious to many students of the dismal science of economics that even the Keynesian approach to economics will not work any more.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I was rather pleased, in a way, to see the people on my immediate right fall into the trap. Their immediate reaction, in effect, was to overturn all the sacred tablets which they had been carrying for many years and to call for a vastly more expansionary kind of budget because, I suppose, if they are the apostles of faith in growth they believe, as does the government, I think, that growth will solve all problems.
We really have to ask ourselves whether the nature of unemployment facing the people of Canada today is of the classical kind. I know there are certain sections of the country where there is massive and very evident unemployment, where the individuals who are thrown out of work feel, at the very least, a certain kind of fellowship in that they see themselves not to be alone. But for many citizens of this country, being unemployed is a lonely, solitary and alienating business because they see themselves as alone out of a job, keenly aware of a sense of uselessness in a society which seems to be busy and bustling all around them.
We really have to ask ourselves whether a purely expansionary budget, in the classical sense, will do anything to change this pattern. The point I am coming to is simply- since I have very little time I would like to dwell on it for my last two or three minutes-that I urge this House, and particularly the government, to take a totally new look at our economy. I urge all hon. members not to fall into the old trap of simply encouraging more growth, because growth by itself will not change the quality of life of Canadians. We must look for a different way of living our economic life in this country. I would urge on this House a policy which concentrates upon qualitative growth as opposed to quantitative growth. We must set out to improve the quality of life for the individual and the community rather than simply the quantity of goods.
There are figures that I could quote. We now know, for example, that 10 per cent of disposable income is saved by Canadians. That is a very high proportion. I do not mean to indicate by this that everybody in Canada has money to save, but there certainly are certain sectors of our population which have money to save. Any simplistic, classically-based expansionary approach to the problem of unemployment will simply give them more money to save, without giving to those people who have not enough money to live on, enough money with which to survive.
We must look at every impetus we put into the economy to see whether it changes the nature of our economic existence. I would urge on the Minister of Finance and on the government a totally new look at the world of work,

because it is becoming very obvious to many people that simply to create jobs as a way of giving people remuneration so that they can buy the goods that we can produce- there is no question that we can produce the goods-will not get them out of the squirrel cage in which they find themselves.
Surely this parliament should be ready to invoke some new thinking rather than simply saying to the country, "Look, we can make the squirrel cage run faster and let those who have drop out, drop out." There are many attendant aspects to what I have said. I am sorry, although I am sure several members are not, that I cannot expand on this matter but I hope that I can on another occasion. Somebody has to stand here and say what a lot of people outside parliament are saying, simply that growth by itself does not change the nature of our existence, that by increasing the gross national product what we are doing in large measure is increasing the production of junk, not changing the quality of our production and the quality of people's lives. What people outside are saying is that the production of junk by a lot of people makes junk out of their lives.
Let us ask ourselves this question as we look at our economy: How many people are truly usefully employed? I end on a note which is not mine, Mr. Speaker. Unlike some other hon. members, I admit that I am plagiarizing. Here I quote from an article by a Mr. Anderson:
Generals are traditionally accused of wanting to re-fight the battles of their youth instead of meeting the weapons or tactics of a current war. The record of politicians (and of many economists) is infinitely worse. They cling tenaciously to techniques devised by their grandfathers to deal with circumstances that have long ceased to exist; and when (as happens sometimes, though not often) a new idea does emerge it is regarded as dangerously novel for at least a generation, and then misapplied.
The new idea that emerged a generation ago was the thinking of Lord Keynes. I am afraid that today it is in danger of being dangerously misapplied because we, the politicians, the representatives of the people of this land, cannot push ourselves into the post-industrial society and cannot begin to realize that the nature of the unemployment beast that faces us has changed radically. We must realize that we must look at the world of work and make sure that henceforward people who do the hard work of this nation are adequately remunerated for it; that there are still many people in this nation, some in this parliament and many in the professions, who are unemployed effectively in terms of real usefulness but nevertheless are extremely well paid. We have to look at the kind of work that is done by the people of Canada. In many cases it is soul-destroying work. In many cases the work we force them to do for remuneration is totally-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as Minister of Consumer and Corporate affairs I would like to draw attention to those features of the budget which are of interest to consumers. This budget is important to consumers. It has a number of provisions which were designed to be of direct benefit to them. The proposed reductions in sales taxes, excise taxes
February 27, 1973

and customs duties will affect a wide range of consumer goods and will have a correspondingly wide impact upon consumers' well-being.
Let me first comment upon the proposed changes in the sales tax. As the House knows, it is proposed to remove the sales tax on confectionaries, chocolate bars, soft drinks, fruit drinks and other near-food products. The effect of this measure in so far as food is concerned will be to exempt from federal sales tax all food and drink for human consumption, except alcoholic beverages.
Furthermore, it is proposed that the federal sales tax will be removed from children's clothing and footwear. These measures will be of great benefit to Canadian consumers, particularly to those in the lower income groups. Already a number of important companies in the food distribution field have announced reductions in the price of soft drinks, fruit drinks, confectionary products and snack foods.
Within one or two days after the announcement of the proposed removal of the sales tax on children's clothing and footwear, several of Canada's leading merchandising organizations announced reductions on the prices of these items. One firm announced a 10 per cent cut, a second announced a 15 per cent cut, while a third made a statement the import of which was that its price reductions would conform completely to the reduced sales tax.
Secondly, Mr. Speaker, the budget proposals include the elimination of the 10 per cent excise tax on cosmetics and toilet articles. Furthermore, it proposes the removal of the excise tax on clocks and watches except those on which the manufacturer's price or duty paid value exceeds $50. These also are constructive proposals from the consumer's point of view and already the benefits are appearing at the point of sale.

speechtext:
Next, Mr. Speaker, let me deal with the benefits to the consuming public from the reductions in customs duties proposed for many articles imported into Canada. The products on which tariff cuts will have the greatest significance for the greatest number of consumers are probably those in the food category. Food prices have been rising more sharply than other consumer prices in recent months, particularly the prices of relatively unprocessed foods. The aim of these cuts is to help moderate those food prices.
Probably the most important food items to be affected by the proposed cuts are fresh beef and veal, fruit juices, bananas and sugar, although several other categories are also involved. The tariff on raw sugar has been reduced, in effect, by 33 cents per hundredweight. Bananas, formerly dutiable at 50 cents per hundredweight, will
The Budget-Mr. Gray
become duty free; duties on fresh beef, veal, pork and certain other fresh meats will be reduced to zero, while the duty on lamb and mutton will be reduced by one-third. Cuts of various amounts are proposed: for canned beef 50 per cent, canned pork 40 per cent, canned hams and other canned meats 25 per cent.
The 10 per cent ad valorem duty on imports of a number of vegetables and fruits will be removed. Thus, duties on these imports will fall to zero except during the season when the Canadian crops come on the market. During this season, these imports will continue to be subject to specific duties of various amounts. The purpose of the proposed cuts is obviously to help moderate prices of the products in question.
Turning now to another matter of continuing concern to Canadian consumers, drug prices, I might recall at this point that the federal government has made a very considerable effort over the past six years to help reduce the price of prescription drugs to Canadians. The proposed reductions in the customs duties on drugs represent a further step in the direction taken by the federal government when it removed the federal sales tax on drugs in 1967. The present proposals provide that customs duties on a wide range of drugs, both prescription and non-prescription, be cut by 50 per cent.
Those who are furnishing their homes or who are setting up housekeeping for the first time will be pleased to know that customs duties will be reduced on vacuum cleaners, washers, carpet sweepers and power lawn mowers. Homemakers will benefit also from the proposed reduction in duties on kitchen or household hollow-ware of aluminum, nickel, iron or steel, as well as the proposed reduction of duties on chinaware and porcelainware.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) in his budget speech on February 19 indicated that the reductions in the sales and excise taxes taken together would reduce federal revenues in the coming fiscal year by about $190 million. It seems likely that the dollar volume of imports which will be affected by the proposed reductions in customs duties may well be of the order of $1.3 billion per year. Mr. Speaker, I think it is clear that the reductions proposed by the Minister of Finance in sales tax, in excise taxes and in customs duties will prove to be advantageous to the Canadian consuming public.
A very basic aim of the budget is to ensure that there is more money in the consumers' wallets and pocketbooks for them to spend. To achieve this aim the government has proposed increases in personal exemptions as well as a substantial cut in personal income tax. This cut involves a 5 per cent reduction in the basic federal income tax up to a maximum of $500. But to ensure that there is meaningful tax relief for the middle and lower income groups, the government has proposed that there be a minimum reduction in personal income tax of $100. This means that the actual tax cuts for many hundreds of thousands of Canadian taxpayers will be far higher than 5 per cent.
For example, as the Minister of Finance has pointed out, taking into account the increase in individual exemption and the cut in personal income tax, for a married couple with two young children and the breadwinner earning $5,000, the total tax will be reduced by $137. This represents a 47 per cent reduction from what the tax

February 27, 1973
The Budget-Mr. Darling
otherwise would have been this year. If this same family has an income of $8,000, the total tax reduction will be $141, or 13 per cent.
As the Minister of Finance said, another way of looking at the effect of these cuts in taxation is to note that a married wage earner with two young children living in any one of the provinces will pay no federal income tax until his income goes above $4,473. Therefore, looking at the 1973-74 fiscal year, Canadian consumers will have available to them an additional $1.3 billion through this reduction in personal income tax. Seventy per cent of this will be in the hands of the majority of Canadian taxpayers-those with an income of less than $10,000. Consumers who are old age pensioners will also benefit from the increase in the basic old age security pension to $100 monthly.
Mr. Speaker, to conclude, I think it is clear that the reductions proposed by the Minister of Finance of sales tax and customs duties as well as the other budget measures-particularly the cut in personal income tax and the increase in the old age pension-will prove and are already proving to be of worth-while benefit to the Canadian consuming public. These measures will help the Canadian economy and at the same time will constitute a countervailing force against inflationary pressures. Therefore, I urge the House to support this budget to ensure that its benefits are in fact available to every Canadian consumer.

Mr. Speaker, at long last, after listening to my colleagues on this side and to other members I have a chance to say a few words. This is my maiden speech, Mr. Speaker, so I would like to begin by congratulating Your Honour on your appointment for another term to the post of Speaker of the House. I would also like to congratulate my colleague, the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave) on his appointment as Deputy Speaker and Chairman of Committees of the Whole House.
May I at this time say I am proud to represent the riding of Parry Sound-Muskoka and to have been selected to follow Mr. Gordon Aiken, Q.C., who was an outstanding member of this House for 15 years.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He served unstintingly in the House until he was forced to retire because of ill health, and I know his many friends here will join with me in wishing him a complete return to health. As an aside, Mr. Speaker, I had a letter from him today and he is enjoying the best health he has had for the past 20 years.
I should like to say a few words about my constituency of Parry Sound-Muskoka. I am sure that many members of this House have been to my region at one time or another and those who have not been so fortunate have heard of the area. My riding is without doubt the finest tourist area in this great Dominion of Canada. This certainly must be so, Mr. Speaker, as more members of this House visit my riding during the summer months than visit all other ridings combined. I might say that one of 
our visitors is His Excellency the Governor General. Tourism is our biggest industry. This can be very good when an area has a strong attraction as a tourist paradise because it brings in people from far and wide. They bring with them not only money but new faces, good will and companionship. The chances are they will enjoy themselves and will tell others. Many of them will build in our area and add to the vitality and prosperity of our region.
These are serious times for our country, Mr. Speaker, and I share the concern expressed by my colleagues who have spoken in the past few days on this budget. These are times that call for leadership and for decision. These are times that call for courage. For that reason I was disappointed, both for myself and for my constituents, at the lack of real evidence in the budget that our country is getting leadership or decision from this government. The only evidence of courage in the budget is the indication that this government is prepared at last to accept some of the recommendations of the official opposition.
I realize that it would have taken courage of a very high order for the present government to bring down a budget that would satisfy the people of Canada rather than the NDP. However, I realize also that it was more expedient, politically, for the government to enter into an arrangement with the NDP in order to prolong its stay in power. This is all the more difficult to accept, Mr. Speaker, and is all the more distasteful when you recall that the official opposition is on record as having told the government that it need not fear defeat so long as it brought down legislation that was meaningful.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) did not offer any deals and he did not propose any arrangements in exchange for personal reward. It was a straightforward announcement of purpose. The government was told that as long as it made a serious effort to govern responsibly and showed signs that it was prepared to grapple with such problems as inflation and unemployment, we in the opposition would act just as responsibly.
It is easy to sit back and criticize. I served as the head of a small municipal government for over a quarter of a century before coming to Ottawa as a new member. Criticizing for the sake of opposing is not good enough. During my campaign I emphasized certain things as priorities which I hoped would be included in the budget, and I thank the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) for those things which were included. The top priorities in my area are, first and foremost, the high cost of living caused by spiralling inflation and the great need for increases in old age pensions for the elderly and many others living on fixed incomes who are hardest hit by inflation.
While the budget does provide some relief for the people in my area, the top priority, to my way of thinking, for the people in rural Canada is to find a way to stop spiralling inflation and the high cost of living. This can only be done by the kind of wage and price freeze suggested by my party earlier in this debate. A great many people in the rural parts of Canada are living on low and fixed incomes. Therefore, they are hardest hit in endeavouring to make their income dollars stretch. This is not the case in the great metropolitan areas where the highest wages are paid and where the great unions are able to demand,
February 27, 1973

and receive, wages which naturally force the cost of goods up. Those of us not so fortunate have to pay for this.
I was pleased, Mr. Speaker, to see the old age pension increased to $100 a month. I still feel, and I know it is the feeling of our party, that this pension should be geared to need. To my way of thinking, the very minimum for all old age pensioners should be $110 a month, with the built-in protection that if the cost of living goes up, the pension goes up automatically.
We are divided into ten provinces, Mr. Speaker, and two great areas, the Yukon and the Northwest Territories. Also there are two other areas, those of the haves and of the have-nots. The have areas are growing like cancers. If the present trend continues, by the year 2000, or sooner, we will have to redraw the map of Canada and throw out the present provincial boundaries. The new map will consist of super areas such as Toronto, Montreal, Winnipeg, Vancouver, Calgary and perhaps our capital city of Ottawa.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And Edmonton.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
All right. Call them what you will, city states, super cities or provinces, these concentrated concrete jungles will have 90 per cent of our population and as much or more of its wealth. The other area or province will be the entire balance of our country and could be named Canada. Let me say a word about redistribution. If we still have the same number of members in this House, those areas will be represented by 238 members and all the rest of Canada by 27.
Something has to be done, Mr. Speaker, to keep people in the rural areas and in towns and villages and to stop this erosion of population to the cities. The top priorities are, as I said before, jobs, housing and control of inflation. In rural Canada today our chief export and most valuable commodity is our young people. We pay to raise and educate them, and then they leave for the great rat race in the monster cities. In recent years some cities have had a twinge of conscience and are now willing to repay us by sending us, in return, their garbage. This pattern of growth means declining populations. It means the underuse of existing local and municipal services. It means an erosion of the municipal tax base. It means under-used school facilities. Something must be done to halt this and provide a way of life to the many people who want to remain in the regions where they were born and raised.
The backbone of the rural areas across our country is the small businessman and enterpreneur who is having a hard job getting by, in making a comfortable living, and who is paying the high wages now demanded and the many other high costs. He is also in a very serious financial position during certain periods of the year. In our particular area, where the economy is buoyant in the summer season, the lean months in the winter eat up the profits and he must borrow money at the bank and pay, in many cases, high interest rates. I feel that low interest rates should be available to these hard working and enterprising citizens who provide the great majority of employment in the many small villages and towns scattered throughout our country.
We have heard much said, Mr. Speaker, during the present session regarding the high water problem in the
The Budget-Mr. Darling
Great Lakes. The entire western boundary of my riding borders on Georgian Bay, and the high water is certainly a serious problem to many tourist and marine operators, as well as to cottagers. They have suffered considerable financial loss. I am hoping that this government will have sufficient funds set aside for emergencies so that it can make a worth-while contribution in conjunction with the province of Ontario.
Let me say a word about the LIP program, Mr. Speaker.
I am aware that the money has now been overspent and a great many applications turned down, some of them very worthy. Having served as a member of a municipal government for a long period, it is my opinion that top priority should have been given to all applications submitted by municipal governments before projects submitted by private individuals or other organizations were considered. If money was left over, it could then have been divided among such individuals or organizations. It is my considered opinion that the elected officials of municipalities know their needs far greater than any individual or organization in the area. I will concede that many worthwhile ones were approved.
I trust that all members of the House who represent constituencies on our coast will pay particular attention to this: they have been daily making life miserable and have been badgering the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) for the tabling of the long-awaited document known as the Darling report. Here it is, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure they will all be delighted with it.
I would be remiss if I did not indicate my pleasure at being able to sit in a parliament with so many colleagues from the Progressive Conservative party. At the same time, I would like to convey my respects to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). Although my colleagues and I may take exception to many of his policies, it is in keeping with the intended spirit of our parliamentary system that when he speaks we afford him the respect due Canada's first minister. I certainly take exception to the way he has been treated time and again.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There has been some doubt expressed as to the wisdom of removing the 11 per cent tax on building supplies. Some hon. members feel that such a measure would provide little relief for the lower income groups. It is true that outside of pure Marxism, equity is an elusive quarry. Nevertheless, repeal of the 11 per cent building supply tax would represent a significant reduction in the final price of a home and allow many more Canadians to own their own home. Apart from the obvious social benefit, a stimulus in the order of $365 million would be injected into the economy. This stimulus, in conjunction with increased sales of building materials and related products, would serve both to boost this sector of the business community and to increase employment in all facets of the housing industry.
At the same time, this policy would serve to dampen the wage demands of workers who have come to view their jobs as uncertain and demand wage rates to compensate for their seasonal nature. This aspect of many of our

February 27, 1973
T7ie Budget-Mr. M. Roy
industries is a prime contributor to our high unemployment rates, inflationary tendencies and outsized Unemployment Insurance Commission payments. In this light, elimination of the 11 per cent tax on building supplies would be a significant step toward a sound economic and a more equitable distribution of funds for all income groups.
I believe I have gone over my time, Mr. Speaker, and I thank you for the consideration shown to me.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have here a letter from Major Guy E. Methot, of the 687th Squadron, dealing with the budget. His squadron totals 170 cadets and its total budget is $800. The cadets have met three times a week, but they must now make up the deficit. These boys have to solicit for funds in all sorts of ways. It seems to me that during the summer months, the Department should seriously consider revising its policy and grant subsidies as well to the girls cadets who, even if they are accepted in theory, do not receive the $3 annual allowance paid to the boys.
Mr. Speaker, that is very dear to me. In my opinion, the Opportunity for Youth Program meets a need, but one must also not forget or underestimate the cadets.
I would like to make a last suggestion concerning the Departments of Public Works and Environment. I am speaking on behalf of many of my colleagues whose ridings border the Des Prairies and Mille-Iles Rivers.
For about 25 years, we have been asking for the canalization of the Des Prairies and Mille-Iles Rivers, in order to avoid happenings unpleasant every spring.
This year, we anticipate heavy flooding on all the lands along the Des Prairies and Mille-Iles Rivers.
As for the Department of Public Works or Environment, I would have been very happy if moneys had been allocated to such works which, in my opinion, and in the opinion of all the other members, are of a great priority for that sector.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time to speak in the budget debate wishing it could have been under different circumstances. The bitter disappointment felt by the people of Canada is beginning to filter through. Editorial comment on the budget is anything but complimentary. There is a feeling of dissatisfaction and bewilderment, and in some quarters downright anger.
My mail since the budget reflects these emotions. One letter from a student doing a school project asked me to explain what the government is doing to reduce unemployment. Another letter tells of a visit to a bank for a loan under the Small Business Loans Act. The writer was told that the bank does not lend money under the act because the interest rate is too low and the bank cannot make a profit at the rate set by the act.
Representatives of several secondary industries have called about tariff cuts and to ask whether this is the forerunner of future cuts to be bargained away at the GATT meeting. It is unfortunate that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) did not consult some of the agricultural associations which will be affected by his tariff cuts on fresh vegetables and fruits. We suspect that the Minister of Finance did not even consult the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). I have received a letter from the proprietor of a small manufacturing company in my riding who writes as follows:
It has been brought to our attention that the proposed budget will decrease the tariff on finished toys while not altering the tariff on components which require further manufacture. If this is the case, then in essence the government is encouraging importers of finished toys at the expense of domestic manufacturers. The toy
The Budget-Mr. Kempling
industry tends to be labour-intensive, and thus I believe an asset to our community and country.
Those are a few of the letters I have received, Mr. Speaker. I am sure you are aware, as I am sure everyone is aware, that many of our secondary manufacturers and secondary industries have not recovered from the accelerated cuts in tariffs in 1972 which were billed as an anti-inflationary measure. I have had numerous conversations with my constituents regarding the game being played by the government and the NDP over the corporate tax cuts and the accelerated depreciation provision in the May, 1972, budget. Is it in the budget, or is it not in the budget? Some say it is, and some say it is not.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Now you see it, now you don't.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Now you see it, now you don't-exactly. But what a game to play with the people who hold the key to employment! According to a press report, the leader of the NDP said he did not want to play dog-in-the-manger over this matter of accelerated depreciation.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He wants to play monkey in the granary.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The names I have heard in reference to that hon. member are not "dog-in-the-manger" and I could not repeat them in this House. The mood of the business men I talk to is one of anger. They had all hoped for a more expansionary budget, one that the business community could grab hold of and begin to display some confidence in the future. Certainly, we would have presented a much more imaginative and forward looking budget, one that would take a real bite out of unemployment and come to grips with inflation.
This government stands condemned by the business community for failing to face the realities of the day. This is the seventh budget this government has presented which was supposed to deal with unemployment and inflation. There seems to be lack of purpose and direction by the government. It is a sort of ad hoc approach to economics filtered through the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis).
The main thrust of this budget seems to be that by cutting income taxes by 5 per cent and raising old age pensions to $100 a month, by dropping the sales tax on children's clothing and candy bars, all this coupled with devaluation of the U.S. dollar will create an internal and external demand for products that will create jobs and thus reduce unemployment. In fact, the government is beginning to hedge on this, because as the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey) said last night:
If there is not enough stimulus for the economy, then in a few months the Minister of Finance can certainly provide more.
I quote that sentence from page 1679 of Hansard, in the event the hon. member wants to raise a point of order. There is no mention in the budget of what position the government will take on small business, secondary industry and the service industries. These businesses collectively are the largest employer in Canada, yet they have no status in the economic life of our country.

February 27, 1973
The Budget-Mr. Kempling
The major problem affecting all business is a continual shortage of money. Let us look back at the havoc caused by the ill-conceived tight money policy of 1969 through 1970 and a part of 1971. The only real winners were the banks. We had inflation, wages went up and the cost of money rose to its highest level in memory. The banks made record profits and, indeed, today have assets of some $60 billion, neatly protected by the Bank Act.
Without exception, the greatest deterrent to business expansion in this country is the lack of money. It is only by expanding the business base that we will make headway toward lowering unemployment. Small businesses, secondary industry and the service industries do not want government grants. They know from long experience that anything the government gives, it must first take away. All they want is access to money at a reasonable rate and they will do the rest themselves. They want less government, not more. They want simplified tax forms and fewer reports to send to the figure filberts at Statistics Canada. In other words, they want the government off their backs.
In my riding there are several small industries. I had a recent call from a businessman who was having a problem with-you guessed it-money. He had orders, but no money. His company had designed a unique hydraulic device that found a ready market in the United States. Our banks could not help him and his company unfortunately became caught in the clutches of the Industrial Development Bank. He was really in trouble then, with orders coming in, demands on cash at a high level, no help from the chartered banks and the IDB charging 12 per cent interest.
With this dilemma facing his company, he met with a group of United States customers and explained his problem. They came back with a solution. The United States customers recommended that he move his manufacturing operations to New York state. They would organize a new company in the United States, give my constituent 49 per cent of the stock, refinance the operation, set up a DISC and ship goods back to Canada. That is what happened.
There are hundreds of similar occurrences, with slight variations, each year in Canada. A lack of money, high interest rates in Canada and plenty of money south of the border at equitable rates is a familiar tune to businessmen. The answer this government gives is that it will set up some conditions and a screening agency, but no mention of solving the real problem. I have mentioned the man in my riding who tried to borrow money from the bank under the Small Businesses Loans Act only to be told he could not borrow money at that rate because the bank could not make a profit at 61 per cent interest. The bank then steered the man to the IDB, which suggested he borrow at 12 per cent interest.
There is nothing in the budget presented on February 19 that will make money any easier for small business, secondary industry and the service industries. There are none of the massive changes in the Income Tax Act promised by minister of finance Benson when Bill C-259 was rammed through this House. These are the same changes echoed by the present minister when he took over the finance portfolio. A few minor changes have been made,

but nothing to make it a workable tax act which the average businessman can understand.
There is no statement of policy by the government as to its over-all plan for secondary industry. In fact, you could easily say this is an anti-business budget. This shows how far to the left this government has gone. The people operating small businesses, secondary industry and service industries in Canada have no status in the economic life of our country. They know how far to the left this government has gone. In spite of being the largest employers and tax contributors, these operators are continually downgraded and held at bay by a government that does not know, does not want to know or just does not give a damn.
The strange part of this indifference by the government is the cost involved. Small business, secondary industry and the service industry want amendments to the Bank Act to ease the flow of money to their operations. Along with everyone else in Canada, they want revisions to the tax act so it is workable, understandable and can be lived with. They want simplified tax forms in keeping with their business records. They want a moratorium on Statistics Canada forms until the value of such forms is proved.
These people want the same access to export credit as large industry. They want an end to the numerous faceless and nameless forms that cross their desks with unintelligible signatures. They want to be able to talk to the faceless and the nameless person who wrote the letter, rather than to be told that he does not accept phone calls. These people want a government with guts enough to face up to the issues of the day, one in which they can have confidence and under which they can plan their business in an orderly fashion and an atmosphere of co-operation.
These requirements would cost the taxpayers nothing, but the budget presented by this government falls way short of expectation, as does the government itself. I cannot support this budget and I join my colleagues and millions of Canadians in condemning this government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity of speaking during the budget debate, but not to dwell on the excellence of the government's budget because there is no need for that. The people in my riding, as well as people across Canada, are already aware of the many measures in this budget that will help the fixed income earner, the low income earner, the old and the young-all of them consumers. The government has indeed put together a package that will receive the approval of a very large majority of Canadians, to the chagrin and frustration of members opposite including the hon. member who has just spoken.
The matters I would like to bring to the attention of several ministers for their immediate consideration and correction have to do with several continuing bureaucratic administrative procedures which frustrate some of our citizens and make my blood pressure rise to boiling point. It is amazing how often parliament adopts a law, with much good will and the best intentions, which is designed to serve the small citizen of this country, yet after the regulations have been compiled by departmental officials it develops that parts of the law become simply bureaucratic nightmares.
February 27, 1973

The first example with which I shall deal is the additional $1,000 personal exemption that was proposed for persons 65 years of age or over for income tax purposes. To all members of this House the meaning was simple and clear. Persons 65 years of age, because they have more medical bills and particular needs because of age, in most cases have no ability for normal earnings and have limited income, should have an additional $1,000 deduction to ensure that their meagre income would not be taxed. To all members it was a simple matter. If it involved a married couple, the additional exemption was two times $1,000, or $2,000. Is this what we have? No. After the officials got through with the income tax forms, it turned out that in order to claim the $2,000 deduction both husband and wife must have earnings of at least $2,500. If only the husband has earnings and the wife simply has her $994.86 old age pension as earnings, her $1,000 additional exemption is useless to her and to her husband.
Again we have a case of gross discrimination. If each one of a couple has earnings of $2,500, their exemption in practical terms can reach over $5,000, but if only the husband has earnings of more then $5,000 the exemptions can reach only $1,000 less. If a way can be found by a bureaucrat to make life hard for the politician, you can bet your life he will find it. In this case they have found a way to make it tough not only for the politician but for the poor, old age pensioner through another example of discrimination which is more helpful to the high income earner than the low income earner. I would therefore ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Stanbury) to quickly correct this injustice.
Another example relates to the deductions allowed a working parent for child care in the amount of $500 per child up to a maximum of $2,000. Again, members accepted this measure with great pleasure and pride, with much good will and the best intentions. However, Mr. Speaker, when the bureaucrats got through with the regulations for this bonanza to working parents, it became a nightmare that frightened away both the parents who needed the relief and the babysitters who are trying to help out. The babysitters want to quit because they become full-time employees. The parents throw up their hands in frustration because they become employers. This involves them in all the implications of unemployment insurance, the Canada Pension Plan, income tax deductions, forms of all sorts, and reports. This disgusts the two parties to the point that the benefit is refused. They would rather not have the help than become involved in all the bureaucracy. Surely a quick, easy and reasonably simple procedure can be found to accommodate these people. Surely we can do away with this nightmare without destroying the value of this measure.
The third point I wish to bring to Your Honour's attention has to do with unemployment insurance. I recognize that Bill C-125 will be in the House shortly and that my recommendations might be more appropriate at that time. But the situation I wish to talk about is in my view so distasteful that I feel a correction must be brought in now. It has to do with the infamous practice of having benefit control officers ask people who are seeking unemploy-
The Budget-Mr. Wise
ment insurance to make statements. The officer interprets the statement, writes the report and has the claimant sign the report as his own. Some officers will ask, "How much do you have to earn to properly support your family?" The claimant will answer, "About $100 a week." The officer will mark on the sheet, "Will not accept less than $100 a week."
The officer then will ask, "Would you take a job in another area?" The claimant will say, "Well, I am established here. I have my family and my house here." The officer will write down, "Will not accept work outside of town." Then he writes, "I am writing these statements knowing exactly what they mean". He turns the sheet to the claimant and says, "Sign here". The claimant is so eager to receive his unemployment insurance benefits that he quickly signs, not knowing he is disqualifying himself completely from benefits.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are right.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will vote for all the amendments the minister presents to prevent abuses in the system. I find the loopholes that were left repugnant and I will support the elimination of abuses as much as possible. However, in this case it is the system that is wrong and abusive. This procedure must cease. If any claimant is to incriminate himself, he should at least be left to do it alone without the help of a benefit control officer. It is a despicable practice. I sometimes ask myself why the control officers have not revolted against this procedure and forced the commission to abandon it. I urge the minister to change this situation, one which is the very opposite of the democratic process and the simple rights of an individual.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He is not here.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He will read about it tomorrow; I will make sure of that. It may be difficult to find a more efficient method to disqualify people from unemployment insurance benefits, but surely the nature of this procedure condemns it outright as an inhuman and unjust one. I urge the minister to quickly dispense with that sort of sordid practice. I have often thought we should have a committee of the House for the purpose of studying the consequences to individuals resulting from regulations which complement our laws. Mr. Speaker, the examples I have brought to your attention confirm the need for such a committee and I commend it to my House leader for consideration.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the first occasion I have had to participate in debate in this House and I sincerely welcome the opportunity. My first wish is to join my fellow hon. members in expressing congratulations to you upon your election to the high office of Speaker, an office in which you conduct yourself so ably, with dignity and a great sense of humour. My congratulations and best wishes are also extended to the Deputy Speaker, the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave), on his elevation to that high post. At this time,

February 27, 1973
The Budget-Mr. Wise
Mr. Speaker, I have a desire to recognize the abilities of two other gentlemen among us, Mr. A. Fraser for his sincere personal interest, and Mr. J. Gordon Dubroy for his keen expertise.
I realize that it is customary for one in my position to spend some time setting forth some of the great virtues of the riding. Realizing that other members wish to speak in this debate, I will not linger in this area at any great length except to inform the House that the riding of Elgin is one that is steeped in some of the most interesting history of our great nation. Elgin, like many other ridings, is a mixture of urban and rural communities. Its industries range in size from a few employees to the giant Ford Company of Canada assembly plant at Talbotville employing between 3,000 and 4,000 people.
A great number of these industries are American-owned and they are excellent corporate citizens. I make that statement without any hesitation, Mr. Speaker. Therefore, any move to restrain or restrict American investment by this or any government would have extremely adverse effects upon the economy of an employment in my riding. Its agriculture is diversified, involving both dairy and beef cattle production. I might say that the Elgin herds possess some of the finest and highest producing cattle that can be found across this country. Food and vegetable growing is very common. We have cash crop production including corn, wheat and beans of many varieties. These are only some of our products.
It is my wish to point out that the single, most valuable crop grown in Elgin is flue-cured tobacco. Its production from Elgin growers alone recently brought in $35 million. When we consider that over $24 million goes for provincial and federal income taxes, and over $551 million for excise tax and duty, one can clearly appreciate the input of the flue-cured tobacco growers and the tobacco industry in our over-all economy. I would be remiss if at a time when I am mentioning some of the aspects of Elgin agriculture I did not draw the attention of hon. members to the world championship awards which were received by my constituents for soybean and tobacco production.
I was pleased to read in the government's estimates that significant amounts of money were granted for the construction of a new post office in the town of Aylmer, and that moneys will be expended on the Lake Erie Harbour of Port Stanley. In a recent conversation which I had with officials of the Department of Public Works regarding damage to the pier at Port Bruce, I was informed that the situation had been investigated, a report was being prepared and the port facilities would be repaired.
I regret that the government continues to ignore the deteriorating harbour, port facilities and property at Port Burwell. I am convinced that the neglect of Port Burwell is clearly a mistake. I make these remarks without fear because I want to draw to the attention of the government the fact that this harbour is within walking distance of the site of the new Dofasco steel plant and hundreds of acres of land have already been purchased for that purpose.
I want to be fair, and without taking too much of hon. members' time I should like to acknowledge with satisfac-

tion those budget items that were welcomed by Canadians across the country. However, the minister and his colleagues can hardly take credit for them because they were measures we had recommended and they had been severely ridiculed by hon. members opposite in many instances and on many occasions.
For many years I have been of the opinion that income tax and tariff legislation governing farmers, farmlands, agricultural products, marketing rights and quotas have been grossly unfair. After studying some of the new proposals relative to these matters, I am convinced of their unfairness. If the reaction I have received is typical of producers across Canada-and I am positive that it is- then this government should well realize its shortcomings in this area. Mr. Speaker, this is another prime example of the lack of understanding, the lack of recognition or the absolute refusal to recognize conditions as they really are. It points to the huge, untravelled distance between those in the ivory towers and those at the grass roots level of this country.
All Canadians have a vital stake in the employment and income-generating potential of the agricultural industry. You will be interested to know that 20 per cent of the gross value of our manufactured goods is supplied by the agricultural industry; 33 per cent of the freight moving through the St. Lawrence Seaway and 20 per cent of the goods moved by our railways are of agricultural origin. How has agriculture performed over the past few years? It is a known fact that the number of farm operators has rapidly declined and their average age has rapidly increased. These are two serious and drastic trends that are still continuing, but they seem to be of little or no concern to this government.
During recent years the output per agricultural worker has increased 100 per cent as compared to 50 per cent for his counterpart, the industrial worker. The consumer has been the major beneficiary of these developments. Today Canadians spend less of their pay on food than ever before, about 19 per cent of the family budget as compared to 28 per cent in France, 24 per cent in the United Kingdom and 37 per cent in Italy. In fact, we Canadians require less of our pay cheques for food than people anywhere except in the United States.
There are two questions that I would like to pose to Canadians in other walks of life. First, what would you do if you had put in the same number of hours of work in your job, or the same effort into your business, but your sales or output dropped by 50 per cent in that year? Second, what would your reaction be if your wages, or prices for products, declined to 50 per cent of those in the previous year? Such things happen to large groups of farmers and are very commonplace in the agricultural industry.
Some of the principal reasons for these problems are poor production incentives, inadequate tariff protection, lack of sufficient export sales promotion and subsidies, and high support prices paid to producers in our traditional markets outside Canada. An example is the fact that in France, barley is subsidized for the export market at $1.23 a bushel more than the Canadian farmer receives for his barley. The average expenditure in agricultural subsidies in Canada per person in 1968 was $350, com-
February 27, 1973

pared to $1,287 in the United States, $1,059 in the United Kingdom and $1,502 in Switzerland. I mention these examples because there is a widening gulf of misunderstanding between farmers and the rest of the economy about the reason and need for assistance to Canadian agriculture.
It is only through an expansive, outward looking agricultural and food policy that the farm sector can ensure that its contribution to the general economy will continue. We need in this budget an energetic and positive program of incentives for our business and industry, both large and small, a program with guidelines which would ensure that public moneys earmarked for the purpose of improving employment truly end up in the creation of more jobs. Too often in the past moneys have ended up in modernization, automation and plant transfers, resulting in even fewer jobs than before.
No mention was made in the budget of lowering the age at which our senior citizens receive their pensions. I am of the opinion that serious consideration should have been given to such a course of action. It is most regrettable that the government has refused to remove the sales tax on building materials. The elimination of this tax would encourage construction and, speaking in human terms, I would remind the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) that construction creates jobs. A glance at the present national unemployment figure in this country would indicate that jobs are still high on the priority list, at least they are on this side of the House.
There are numerous other areas of concern that I would have liked to talk about at length tonight, but because of the limited time available I will be unable to do so. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I have submitted these words with sincerity and genuine concern, and will continue to do so on future occasions for as long as I have the good fortune and the honour to represent in the House of Commons the great people of Elgin.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take this occasion to make a few comments on the budget.
It is rather interesting, Mr. Speaker, to listen to a series of speeches on a budget which, according to some, seems to be the solution to all our problems and, according to others, seems to be the worst budget ever introduced and would have no beneficial effect.
I should like to express in an unbiased manner, as I always attempt to do, very honest opinions in respect of this budget. It is certainly not as great and not as good as some hon. members would have us believe, though it is not as bad as some other hon. members, in view of their opinions, tried to make us believe.
The outstanding points and objectives of this budget are of course to lower the unemployment rate and stimulate more rapid growth, to reduce inflationary pressures, also, and deaden the effects of past inflation, to increase actual income and to assure elderly Canadians or a more equitable share of the country's prosperity, and, lastly, to work towards a better balanced economic development of all regions of Canada.
The Budget-Mr. La Salle
How far will this budget allow us to carry out all of these objectives. I am not as optimistic as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), who believes and claims that these measures will create 300,000 jobs. In any case, I hope that whoever estimated that 300,000 jobs could be created are not the same people who dreamt up the 100,000 jobs that the government of Quebec promised us a few years back, or the other 100,000 jobs that the building of an airport at Saint-Scholastique was guaranteed to provide. We know very well how wrong those forecasts were, and I trust, Mr. Speaker, that those responsible for the estimates in this budget are not the same people.
Taken as a whole, of course, the budget is not as bad as some would have us believe. The budget is definitely the product of a minority government. That is nothing new, and I have said several times before that a minority government could achieve in six months what a majority government has failed to achieve or could not achieve in four years. We see the government having to do more and better, when forced to act. In my opinion, the opposition should join forces to force the government to fulfil the people's hopes and needs.
The budget now under consideration is much more worthwhile than those of past years and I must say objectively that I will support it in spite of its deficiencies as most measures are generally deficient in one way or another. It remains nevertheless that this budget on the whole has some merit and that in my opinion it is preferable to support it rather than to reject it.
I could also dwell on some commitments in this budget concerning a basic exemption for taxpayers which will increase from $1,500 to $1,600 and an exemption for a married couple which will augment from $2,850 to $3,000. Moreover, the basic federal income tax will be reduced by 5 per cent and the personal income tax rate will be escalated from 1974. We are pleased also with the $18 monthly increase in old age security pensions.
I regret to see that the government has not seriously considered giving the old age security pension to people who are 60. We could at least have given it progressively over a period of 5 years, as was the case when the eligibility age was brought down from 70 to 65; I think we could also have thought of giving the old age security pension to the spouse of the beneficiary, even if he or she is not yet 65.
I think it is important to remind hon. members and the minister in particular of the problem that arises for an old couple, when one is not yet 65 and could get $170, when we know perfectly that a couple both aged 65 will be able to get $325 a month.
I think it will be important for all hon. members, when new bills issued from this budget will be brought in to propose the necessary amendments, and if we failed to legislate in order to control unemployment, I think I would not hesitate to remind them of the importance of bringing in amendments designed to force the government to give the old age security pension at 60, even if it is done progressively over a period of 5 years, if it appeared impossible for the government to do it quicker. I think that if we seriously want to find a solution to the problem of unemployment, this kind of measure would be quite right.

February 27, 1973
The Budget-Mr. La Salle
I recognize that the government made a tremendous effort to reduce unemployment by injecting new credits into the economy but after five years we realize not only that the rate of unemployment has not diminished but that it even has a tendency to grow. Now, I think it is the duty, the government to improve the social climate: what better way of doing it than by giving holidays to people who have reached an age when they deserve them? Of course, some will tell me that it will be extremely costly for the government to give the old age security pension as early as at 60.
I should like to put this question to the Minister of Finance: How much does it cost to provide for 500,000 to
600,000	unemployed, for instance? If the required calculations were made to grant the old age security pension as early as at 60 years of age, on an optional basis for some months and shortly after on a compulsory basis, we would finally achieve a truly acceptable social policy. Of course, people would become unemployed at 60, but they would be happy unemployed, thanks to a decent pension, contrary to our 20-year old unemployed who are rather inclined to be revolutionary. To my mind, the government always errs in a masterly manner when it applies itself to increasing the benefits and allowances of those who make up a generation we are in the process of spoiling.
In my opinion, it rests with the Opposition members, especially under the present circumstances, owing to the membership of the House, to suggest amendments to the bills which will be referred to us. The official opposition should make a point of introducing constructive measures and I would like to see the New Democratic Party take position on such proposals. Up to now, I somewhat regret the lack of aggressiveness of the New Democratic Party which is too readily approving the budget.
Once again, I admit as many others do that it contains some good provisions; moreover, on the whole, I will support the passage of the budget, because it contains a minimum of good provisions.
I heard this afternoon a member of the New Democratic Party say that if he had been a government member, he would have done better. But is there anything preventing the New Democratic Party from proposing positive amendments? The Progressive Conservative party has proposed an amendment, the Social Credit party has proposed a sub-amendment, but the New Democratic party has proposed no amendment. We could have made some evaluation of an amendment, voting for or against it.
I believe it important for the opposition parties not to subject The New Democratic party to difficulties, but to allow it to support a measure that would improve the lot of our older citizens. We do know that that party has always paid much attention to the older or the poorer citizens, and I believe that it would be very interesting to know about the amendments and suggestions that could be introduced in this House inviting the New Democratic party, as all the other opposition parties, to force the government to act, because the Canadian people know very well that the opposition is in a position to do so. No doubt the government will not allow itself to be defeated on a positive and worthwhile measure. We all know that 
the government is obliged to come to some arrangements and that it also pays heed to positive solutions or suggestions. Therefore, I consider it my duty to invite the opposition parties to discharge their primary responsibilities, forcing the government to improve the legislation placed before us.
I do not hesitate to say that the $20 increase in old-age security payments is welcome by those who can get it, but, there again, I believe that we would have benefited from lowering the eligibility age in order to make some room for the unemployed and for the young people waiting openings on the labour market.
For instance, I would have been happy if this budget had provided some moneys for amateur sports. I know that the Speech from the Throne says that amateur sports could eventually obtain some additional credits. When this government talks about youth's motivation toward physical fitness, I wonder to what point it is serious. A year and a half ago, I suggested to the Minister to grant some very special funds enabling municipalities to acquire the basic tools. But what are those basic tools? Whether one is talking about physical fitness, financial participation, direct or indirect, to the 1976 Olympic Games, youths must still be offered training facilities. But basic tools in municipalities mean arenas, playgrounds, lighting systems, public swimming pools, etc. How can municipalities acquire these? If they were acquired, I am convinced that volunteerism would follow, that interested people would offer to participate, and that at last we would set up facilities so that youths may acquire that physical fitness which is absolutely required.
I thought that the federal government was in a position to bring in a tripartite policy at the financial level. There should be no cheating, of course. The municipalities could ask the province to supply 25 p. cent, contribute themselves 25 p. cent and let the federal government pay the other half of the expenses incurred for the project.
In that way, we would not infringe upon the provincial jurisdictions and the fact that the municipality would be compelled to make a request to its province would enable the latter to adjust its planning at leisure. So, if the province accepts to pay 25 p. cent of the cost of an arena or of a public swimming pool, the federal government would pay 50 p. cent of the expenditures, would respect at the same time the provincial jurisdiction, would leave the province free to monitor the planning, the municipality would show its interest and good will by paying 25 p. cent of the cost of the project. I think this would be a way to prove that the federal government is willing to help youth in need of physical training.
