speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in 1789 social needs were vital in France and Marie Antoinette responded to the cries of the French people for bread with, "Let them eat cake." In 1973 the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) meets the cries for employment, decent housing and the alleviation of poverty in Canada with, "Let them eat candy and drink pop". When we examine this budget closely, we see it for what it really is, a tale full of
February 27, 1973

sound and fury, signifying nothing. It purports to improve the lot of Canadians on fixed incomes by raising the old age pension by what appears to be $18 a month; in reality is a mere $15 per month.
We in the New Democratic Party find the increase a half-hearted response to the needs of our people who exist on fixed incomes. Even though it is a crumb, we will accept it. What were the Tories prepared to offer the pensioner? During the October election campaign that party was prepared to raise the basic old age pension to $90 a month. Since the election they have suddenly discovered the old age pensioners and are now calling for a greater increase than the government has proposed. It only serves to show that the Tories are just as opportunistic as the Liberals. But we must not forget that these two corporate parties have now entered a new era of disincentives for the poor and incentives for their corporate friends and allies. After all, the Liberals and the Conservatives would not want over one million Canadians, 65 years old and over, becoming lazy with large pension cheques.
Another crumb is in the area of personal taxes, where the government broke with the traditional concept of across the board tax cuts. The budget proposes a minimum $100 cut in tax. We accept this crumb also. The indexing system proposed is a small step in the right direction-another crumb, and we accept it. Apart from these meagre offerings forced out of this government, the rest of the budget does not deal seriously with unemployment and the urgent social needs of the Canadian people. On the contrary, the selective federal sales tax cuts might very well find their collective way into corporate pockets. We warn the government that the day will come when the people of Canada will want to eat at the table and will not be content with crumbs. They will want to share in the meal. Then these two old-line parties can exist side by side as the corporate concubines they really are.
The list of items on which the federal sales tax has been lifted indicates, first of all, that the government is not interested in the production and availability of necessary goods such as building materials and adult clothing. These members to my right, Mr. Speaker, would suggest that the 11 per cent federal sales tax on building materials be dropped. I should like to ask them why they would not use their influence with the premier of the province of Ontario to get that government to drop the 5 per cent sales tax on building materials, if they are so interested in stimulating the building market.
Stimulation of the consumer market, as I have mentioned, Mr. Speaker, would certainly have served to create employment opportunities so vital to the nation's economy today. By what logic is the tax on candy and pop removed, and not the tax on building materials? Even if the saving is passed on to the consumer, how does the Minister of Finance justify stimulating consumerism in a non-essential area? I grant that the selective federal sales tax on various items has been reduced, but what assurance have we that these decreases will result in savings to the Canadian people? The government has refused to implement any kind of monitoring system to ensure that the Canadian people get the benefit of these sales tax cuts. The minister seems to have blind faith that the market-
25789-37i
The Budget-Mr. Demers
place of the free enterprise system will lower prices to the Canadian people. Alas for such faith! We know from past experiences that when the federal sales tax on prescription drugs was dropped by the last minority government- that was another crumb-the people never received the benefit. So why do we think we are going to receive benefits now?
If the minister is interested in dealing with one of Canada's most serious problems, why not provide a tax rebate to individuals who build their own homes or have their homes built for them? It seems to me that two problems would have been attacked by such a tax incentive, namely, unemployment and inflation. While the budget indicates the extent to which the Liberals are willing to tinker with the economy, it also exposes their opportunism and inability to effectively redirect the human, financial and natural resources of our country so that poverty may be eliminated and a better quality of life may emerge for the Canadian people as a whole.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the budget brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) on Monday, February 19, 1973, is considered by the vast majority of financial analysts as a masterpiece.
Its main objective is to check unemployment. But its strength, and this is what most surprises those financial analysts, lies in the fact that in addition to checking unemployment the budget also considerably dampens the effects of inflation.
Normally, in our North American economic context, when unemployment goes down, inflation goes up. By decreasing inflation, one creates more unemployment.
By reducing income tax, not only in the lower income brackets but also in the average income levels, the budget gives Canadians more purchasing power. Automatically our industries will have to produce more; they will therefore require more labour.
What I admire most in this budget is that the average-income group will also benefit from tax reductions. We often think about the Canadian middle class. Unfortunately, every time this happens, it is for the purpose of paying more taxes, indirect taxes as well as municipal and school taxes.
I even know about administrators who are looking for new ways of increasing taxes in future. This middle class which is made up of workers form the greater part of Duvernay. They are people who contribute heavily to all levels of the Canadian economy.
Finally in this budget the minister of Finance has shown that this middle class is also representing the overtaxed silent majority, to such an extent that many are discouraged in seeing such a large share of their working hours wasted on taxes of all kinds.
It must be remembered that, basically, our economy leans on the middle class which must be encouraged as best we can. It is due to these people that our gross national product is so high and that we are in a position to improve our social assistance such as old age security

February 27, 1973
Adjournment Debate
pensions, unemployment insurance benefits, social welfare benefits, etc.
I said earlier this budget is intended to stop inflation to some extent.
In fact, by reducing the sales tax on several products, especially on children's clothing and shoes of all kinds for young people, there results an appreciable reduction of the family cost of living.
Indeed, I should have preferred to see an increase in family allowances, but the elimination of the sales tax is equivalent to an indirect increase of those allowances.
The budget provides for the Canadian taxpayer tax cuts varying from $100 to $500 a year. This reduction, which increases purchasing power, will also contribute somewhat to bringing down salary increases, a primary cause of inflation in this country.
A decrease in tax rates equivalent every year to the percentage of inflation has also been provided, a provision that will, I believe, most effectively curb the inflationary pressure. I shall clarify my statement.
In the late 50's, a construction worker earned an average of $100 a week. Now, hourly rates have gone slightly over $5 an hour for a 40-hour week, bringing present salaries slightly over $200 a week. Thus, in 14 years, salaries of those workers have doubled, from $5,200 to $10,400 a year. After payment on taxes on a salary of $5,200, a married, childless workers was left with a purchasing power of $4,300. Today, with a salary of $10,400, the purchasing power in the same case is only $8,100. Salaries have therefore doubled whereas taxes, because of increased rates, have gone $500 over double their amount.
These calculations therefore show that the progressive tax rate has substantially contributed to inflation during the past decade and that during the past 13 or 14 years the increase in tax rates accounted for some 20 per cent of inflation in Canada.
In order to curb this effect, there will be an indexing of personal income taxes as of January 1, 1974, in order to halt the erosion of purchasing power.
I should also like to point out another cause of inflation, the collective agreements which, over the past ten years-

subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-ALLEGED EXCLUSION OF GAGETOWN FROM BASES SHARING FUNDS FOR LABOUR-INTENSIVE PROJECTS
NATIONAL DEFENCE-ALLEGED EXCLUSION OF GAGETOWN FROM BASES SHARING FUNDS FOR LABOUR-INTENSIVE PROJECTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 22 I asked the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) if he could tell the House why base Gagetown

in New Brunswick was omitted from the 40 bases sharing the $13.3 million allotted for federal labour intensive projects. I have referred previously to my concern about the increasing rate of unemployment in New Brunswick and in particular to the alarming rate of increase in my own constituency, York-Sunbury. The largest employer of unskilled and semi-skilled labour in New Brunswick is Canada's largest military training establishment, base Gagetown.
I believe that several hundred thousand dollars was requested by the authorities at base Gagetown under the winter works program to carry out much needed maintenance on defence properties, including accommodation occupied by military personnel and their dependants. I would like to ask the Minister of National Defence why, with such a large rate of unemployment in that particular area and the obvious wastefulness of allowing valuable properties to continue depreciating, he would select base Gagetown as one of the few military stations to receive absolutely no grant from his allotment of $13.3 million.
As part of the program of work that was proposed from base Gagetown involved a large portion of labour-intensive work on armouries and other defence properties throughout New Brunswick, it would seem that other hard-hit communities in my province have also been deprived of this opportunity for employment, opportunities that have been given to all other provinces except Alberta, the Yukon and the Northwest Territories.
I ask the minister to reconsider what appears to me and to the people of my constituency to be a case of unfair discrimination in the allocation of funds placed at his disposal. Urgently needed work has to be done at base Gagetown and a large number of men, most of them heads of families, are willing and able to do it.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (President of the Treasury Board):
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-ALLEGED EXCLUSION OF GAGETOWN FROM BASES SHARING FUNDS FOR LABOUR-INTENSIVE PROJECTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was perhaps incorrect to direct this question to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) because he does not have total discretion in the matter. If the hon. member will recollect, during the discussion on the $350 million winter works program an allocation of this sum of money was made across the country by provinces in relation to population, the rate of unemployment and the degree of seasonality of unemployment. It was hoped there would ensue a fair distribution of this money.
At the same time, the government set aside-this was subsequently approved in the supplementary estimates- the sum of $60 million in a Treasury Board vote for direct employment through the federal government for federal labour-intensive programs. The moneys were allocated by provinces in exactly the same way, using the same criteria as the federal winter works program, the larger program. Departments were then invited to submit proposals for work showing the cost, the type of project and the number of man-hours, from which it was possible to grade them in order of number of people employed per dollar expended or number of dollars required to secure one man-month of employment. The allocation of funds was made by provinces in accordance with the formula suggested by the provinces in respect of the $60 million and in relation
February 27, 1973

to those projects which would produce the greatest number of man-months per dollar expended.
In the case of the camp Gagetown projects, the number of man-months employed for the given number of dollars expended tended to be higher than others. For this reason, Gagetown was not selected. I sympathize with the hon. member because there is unemployment there, but the money could not usefully be used; it could more profitably and more urgently be employed elsewhere.

subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-RETIRED PUBLIC SERVANTS, ARMED FORCES PERSONNEL AND RCMP PENSIONS-STATUS OF CONSIDERATION OF RAISING OR REMOVING CEILING ON ESCALATION
SOCIAL SECURITY-RETIRED PUBLIC SERVANTS, ARMED FORCES PERSONNEL AND RCMP PENSIONS-STATUS OF CONSIDERATION OF RAISING OR REMOVING CEILING ON ESCALATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday, January 24, as recorded at page 610 of Hansard, I put this question to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury):
In view of the assurance given by the minister toward the end of the previous session that consideration would be given to raising or removing the 2 per cent ceiling on the escalation of pensions of retired public servants and also retired armed forces and RCMP personnel, can the minister say what is now the status of that consideration?
The President of the Treasury Board replied:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the genesis of the 2 per cent figure in the Superannuation Act, namely, its relationship to the Canada Pension Plan, perhaps these two matters could be looked at together.
I then asked a supplementary question which raised another issue in the same field. As the President of the Treasury Board knows, I am concerned about both issues. The second issue was that of the position of retired armed forces and RCMP personnel who are under 60 years of age and have to wait until that point before the escalation of their pensions begins. As the President of the Treasury Board knows, it has been my argument for some time, particularly since certain changes were made regarding early retirement, that such personnel should not have to wait until age 60 to start drawing their escalation.
However, let me concentrate this evening on the removal of the 2 per cent ceiling on escalation of the pensions we are speaking about tonight. As the minister knows, the first escalation of pensions was on the old age pension, and it was subject to a 2 per cent ceiling. But we make progress, even when the Liberals are in power, and we have now got to the point where old age and certain other pensions are escalated by the actual percentage rise in the cost of living. Indeed, we have gone a step further: there is now on the table of the House a report from the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs which recommends that war disability pensions be escalated by an even more beneficial factor, namely, the wage index, and I emphasize the fact that that is higher than the cost of living index. That, in my book, is a wonderful report and a tremendous recommendation, and we shall get to it later in this session.
In light of the progress that is being made, I think it is unfair to retain for retired public servants and retired members of the RCMP and armed forces the 2 per cent ceiling, so that no matter by how much the cost of living goes up in a year their pensions cannot go up more than 2 per cent. I got back to the minister on this question again
Adjournment Debate
on Friday, February 9. I thought I made a good point, but all he did was look at me while the Speaker called order. On another occasion, namely, on February 12, I drew attention to the fact that figures which had been tabled that day showed a tremendous increase in the amount of money in the special fund out of which these escalation payments are made, to which the minister responded that this additional money had to be looked at as providing for a greater charge on the fund in later years.
Time is at a premium but I should like to argue with the minister on that point. I went back over the debate in 1970-even though I remembered it quite well-and I found no suggestion that this fund for escalating the pensions of retired public servants and others was to be put on an actuarial basis. The key sentence of the then President of the Privy Council, the present Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald), is to be found at page 4589 of Hansard for March 10, 1970, and is as follows:
These increases will in turn be financed by additional contributions of one half of one per cent by present employees, contributions that will be matched by the government.
As the minister knows, every time we have been faced with complaints by present employees that they have to pay this one half of one per cent in order to pay for the escalation of pensions received by those who are now retired, our answer-the minister's and mine-has been that when they get to the point of retirement the working public servants of that day will pay one half of one per cent to provide for the escalation of their pensions.
I feel that there is nothing in the record to indicate that this fund is on an actuarial basis. It is on a current or pay-as-we-go basis. I contend that, partly because the fund is growing rapidly, but even more so because of what is right-namely, that it is unfair to retain this 2 per cent ceiling-early action should be taken either to raise that ceiling to a much higher figure, or to put it on the basis of the actual cost of living or remove it altogether and accept the formula recommended by the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs.
I do not expect the minister to stand up tonight, give me the perfect answer and say, "Yes, we shall get at this tomorrow morning and bring in the legislation tomorrow afternoon." But I do urge him to activate consideration of this matter. If it requires further consultation with representatives of the staff associations, for goodness sake let us have that consultation right away. 1 ask the minister not to wait until something is done about the Canada Pension Plan, because that involves federal-provincial relations and the minister knows how long that can take. In the meantime, it is only fair and just for retired public servants, and retired armed forces and RCMP personnel that their pensions should be accelerated every year by at least the rise in the cost of living.
Therefore I urge that steps be activated now so we can get rid of that 2 per cent ceiling, and I hope while he is at it the minister will take steps to get rid of the unfairness in respect of retired armed forces and RCMP personnel who are under age 60.

February 27, 1973
Adjournment Debate

NATIONAL DEFENCE-JERICHO LAND, VANCOUVER- INQUIRY AS TO CALLING OF TENDERS CONCERNING DISPOSAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 26 I asked the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) a question concerning a property commonly known as the remaining 38 acres of Jericho defence land in the city of Vancouver lying north of Fourth Avenue. My question asked whether the government was making plans to sell this land. The minister's answer was that his predecessor indicated that if the city wished to reopen negotiations, because there was already an agreement with the city of Vancouver, the city could do so. He seemed puzzled that I should think they were going to sell this land, although the terms of the agreement, as I will show in a minute, with the city of Vancouver provided that the government could sell it.
There have been many briefs, hearings and discussions in respect of this land. I think it would be worth while to run through the history in respect of this land. Prior to World War II the land was used for recreational purposes by the city of Vancouver as a golf course and beach land. During the war, in 1942, the Department of National Defence acquired the use of the land primarily by lease and the citizens of Vancouver were willing to give up their recreational land as part of the war effort, particularly since the government assured them it would be returned after the war.
In 1947, instead of having the land returned, it was purchased by the federal government. There were several parcels, but they ended up with a total package of 172 acres. Then followed 20 years of discussions, meetings and letters. During the 1968 election campaign, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) landed on the land by helicopter for an election rally. He assured the voters or perhaps he mislead them-but in any event they received the impression they were not to worry about the Jericho land and that the government would certainly be returning it to the citizens of Vancouver.
In 1969, the agreement with the city was entered into which provides that 72 of the 172 acres would come to the citizens for park-land and 38 acres would be sold by the federal government in order to recover the cost of relocating the military installation. The agreement fails to mention, and the government certainly has not often mentioned it recently, that they still retained 62 acres south of Fourth Avenue. That is the situation today.
In 1971, certain groups of concerned citizens who realized this was not the best use of land in the city of Vancouver formed what is known as the Jericho Parks Committee. The membership is made up of representatives of 17 citizens' groups from the whole of the lower mainland of British Columbia. I was involved with this group during 1972. I took the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) there. It was agreed that a Conservative government certainly would return the land to the citizens of Vancouver for park use for the price of $1. In May, 1972, Mr. Benson, the then minister of national defence, said that the government would certainly part with the 38 acres, but wanted money for it. My Liberal opponent during the election campaign said he was cer-
February 27, 1973

tain Vancouver would get the land back. We will come to the matter of price in a moment.
Today the Vancouver paper carries a report that the parks board chairman has been to Ottawa and has spoken to officials here, I assume in the Department of National Defence, and that he finds the government now is asking questions such as, how does the city propose to use the land? I also find that he took back the date of March 6 when a final decision is expected by the government. But I am in Ottawa and I do not know what goes on in our area except by reading the papers.
Let us talk about price. In 1965, when the government first decided it would dispose of the Jericho lands, the price talked about was $12 million. Later, when we were about to have an election, the price being talked about by the government was $41 million. In this day of inflation that is wonderful. That was for 110 acres, the whole of the section north of Fourth Avenue. By October, 1972, we were down, according to my Liberal opponent, to a price of about $500,000.
Let us talk about the moving cost. Certainly the government had to move the installation, but that was its choice. It certainly is not reasonable to have the citizens of Vancouver paying for an inevitable move that the government chose to make. Our Conservative defence critic told me that after his research he found that some two dozen similar cases existed in Canada and in most instances the investment by the government had been written off in the year of purchase.
The government still has the 62 acres on the south side of Fourth Avenue about which I have spoken. The latest blow, I believe, to the citizens of Vancouver happened two weeks before the election when the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) announced in Toronto that the federal government would give a gift of 86 acres of farm land to the citizens of Toronto at a cost of $30 million. The people of Vancouver wondered if they were still in Canada. Vancouver's reward for its contribution to the war effort in giving up the use of its land is to end up fighting the federal government in order to get it back. The government has no right to be there, and they make
Adjournment Debate
much of not charging us any taxes during the time they were there and making grants in lieu. We have been deprived of the use of our land for all these years, and we think we should be charging the government for the loss of its use.

speakeroldname: Mr. Leonard Hopkins (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-JERICHO LAND, VANCOUVER- INQUIRY AS TO CALLING OF TENDERS CONCERNING DISPOSAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not in the middle of an election campaign; I am just delivering an official answer for the Department of National Defence.
The hon. member's representation on behalf of his constituency of Vancouver Quadra and the city of Vancouver is one that he has been most assiduous in pursuing. I note that on January 12 he placed a private member's notice of motion on the order paper concerning this subject. This was done following a very detailed reply by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) in a letter to the hon. member dated January 3, 1973. At that time the hon. member was advised that there are no immediate plans to dispose of the 38-acre development area although such disposal is part of the understanding with the city of Vancouver.
In the same letter the minister enclosed a detailed departmental position paper on the whole subject of the Jericho beach lands. This was done to provide the member with the whole background of the subject, as there has obviously been much local misinterpretation of this issue. Further, on January 26 the minister, in response to a question in the House from the hon. member, as recorded at page 685 of Haiisard, confirmed the departmental position.
Basically, the department made an agreement with the city of Vancouver whereby 78 acres of waterfront land at Jericho beach was turned over to the city of Vancouver for $1. The remaining property, some 38 acres, was to be sold by the department. This agreement is still in effect. The basic departmental position is that if the city of Vancouver wishes to reopen this agreement, the minister is prepared to listen to any official representations that may be made.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10.26 p.m.

Wednesday. February 28, 1973
